It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation: Not long after, the Patriarch once again occupied his seat, and the assembly listened as he explained the principles of the doctrine. Using an analogy, he was discussing the process of cultivating the "flesh skin" outside the body. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey approached, kowtowing, and said, "Disciple is here." The Patriarch asked, "What have you been cultivating for the past few years?" The Monkey replied, "Recently, my understanding of the dharma nature has become clearer, and my fundamental root has become more solid." The Patriarch said, "You have achieved clarity of dharma nature and have grasped the fundamental root, and yet, you still have to be wary of the 'three calamities'." The Monkey listened, and after deliberating for a long time, said, "The Patriarch's words are in error. I often hear that the great virtuous ones abide by the heavenly virtue and coexist with heaven, that the water and fire are in harmony, and that all sicknesses are eliminated. How can there be the three calamities?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary path: it involves obtaining the creative power of heaven and earth, and secretly penetrating the profound principle of the sun and moon. Although one may possess an elixir body and a long lifespan, after five hundred years, a thunder calamity will be sent by heaven to strike you. You must cultivate awareness and discernment beforehand, and use them to avoid the calamity. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will be as long as heaven's, but if you fail to avoid it, you will meet your demise. Another five hundred years later, a fire calamity will be sent by heaven to burn you. This fire is not the fire of heaven, nor is it ordinary fire, but rather the 'yin fire.' It will begin to burn from the Moshan spring, right through the Muddy Palace, and reduce your five viscera to ashes, causing your four limbs to wither away. After another five hundred years, a wind calamity will be sent by heaven to blow you away. This wind is not the wind from the east, south, west, or north, nor is it the gentle, golden, or spring wind, but rather the 'assassin wind.' It will enter your skull through the fontanel, pass through your six cavities, go through the dan field, pierce the nine apertures, and consume your flesh and bones. This is why you must avoid them all." The Monkey listened, and his very bones trembled with fear. He kowtowed and prayed, "The venerable Patriarch, who is full of compassion, has transmitted to me the method to avoid the three calamities. I shall not forget your mercy." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult. You simply differ from others, so I couldn't teach it to you." The Monkey said, "I also have a round head that touches the heavens, and feet that are square and plant firmly on the ground, with nine apertures and four limbs, and five viscera and six cavities, what's the difference?" The Patriarch said, "You may resemble people in appearance, but you lack a cheekbone." The Monkey's face was indeed misshapen, with a hollowed-out cheek and a pointed chin. The Monkey reached out to touch his cheek, laughing and said, "The Patriarch's words are not well-considered. I may lack a cheekbone, but I have a larger mouth, which can also accommodate more saliva." The Patriarch said, "Fine. What method of cultivation do you want to learn?" The Monkey said, "I want to learn one form of the general catastrophe method." The Patriarch said, "Since you want to learn, come closer and I will teach you the oral formula." He leaned in close and whispered something incomprehensible to the Monkey. This Monkey King also became enlightened at that moment, and when he mastered the oral formula, he practiced and cultivated himself, eventually mastering all seventy-two forms of catastrophe transformation.
source_text: 却早过了三年，祖师复登宝座，与众说法。谈的是公案比语，论的是外像包皮。忽问：“悟空何在？”悟空近前跪下：“弟子有。”祖师道：“你这一向修些什么道来？”悟空道：“弟子近来法性颇通，根源亦渐坚固矣。”祖师道：“你既通法性，会得根源，已注神体，却只是防备着‘三灾利害’。”悟空听说，沉吟良久道：“师父之言谬矣。我常闻道高德隆，与天同寿，水火既济，百病不生，却怎么有个三灾利害？”祖师道：“此乃非常之道：夺天地之造化，侵日月之玄机；丹成之后，鬼神难容。虽驻颜益寿，但到了五百年后，天降雷灾打你，须要见性明心，预先躲避。躲得过，寿与天齐，躲不过，就此绝命。再五百年后，天降火灾烧你。这火不是天火，亦不是凡火，唤做‘阴火’。自本身涌泉穴下烧起，直透泥垣宫，五脏成灰，四肢皆朽，把千年苦行，俱为虚幻。再五百年，又降风灾吹你。这风不是东南西北风，不是和薰金朔风，亦不是花柳松竹风，唤做‘赑风’。自囟门中吹入六腑，过丹田，穿九窍，骨肉消疏，其身自解。所以都要躲过。”悟空闻说，毛骨悚然，叩头礼拜道：“万老爷垂悯，传与躲避三灾之法，到底不敢忘恩。”祖师道：“此亦无难，只是你比他人不同，故传不得。”悟空道：“我也头圆顶天，足方履地，一般有九窍四肢，五脏六腑，何以比人不同？”祖师道：“你虽然像人，却比人少腮。”原来那猴子孤拐面，凹脸尖嘴。悟空伸手一摸，笑道：“师父没成算！我虽少腮，却比人多这个素袋，亦可准折过也。”祖师说：“也罢，你要学那一般？有一般天罡数，该三十六般变化，有一般地煞数，该七十二般变化。”悟空道：“弟子愿多里捞摸，学一个地煞变化罢。”祖师道：“既如此，上前来，传与你口诀。”遂附耳低言，不知说了些甚么妙法。这猴王也是一窍通时百窍通，当时习了口诀，自修自炼，将七十二般变化，都学成了。

human_translations.translator_1: Three years went by swiftly, and the Patriarch again mounted his throne to lecture to the multitude. He discussed the scholastic deliberations and parables, and he discoursed on the integument of external conduct. Suddenly he asked, “Where’s Wukong?” Wukong drew near and knelt down. “Your pupil’s here,” he said. “What sort of art have you been practicing lately?” the Patriarch asked. “Recently,” Wukong said, “your pupil has begun to apprehend the nature of all things and my foundational knowledge has become firmly established.” “If you have penetrated to the dharma nature to apprehend the origin,” said the Patriarch, “you have, in fact, entered into the divine substance. You need, however, to guard against the danger of three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, he thought for a long time and said, “The words of the master must be erroneous. I have frequently heard that when one is learned in the Way and excels in virtue, he will enjoy the same age as Heaven; fire and water cannot harm him and every kind of disease will vanish. How can there be this danger of three calamities?” “What you have learned,” said the Patriarch, “is no ordinary magic: you have stolen the creative powers of Heaven and Earth and invaded the dark mysteries of the sun and moon. Your success in perfecting the elixir is something that the gods and the demons cannot countenance. Though your appearance will be preserved and your age lengthened, after five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of thunder to strike you. Hence you must be intelligent and wise enough to avoid it ahead of time. If you can escape it, your age will indeed equal that of Heaven; if not, your life will thus be finished. After another five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of fire to burn you. That fire is neither natural nor common fire; its name is the Fire of Yin, and it arises from within the soles of your feet to reach even the cavity of your heart, reducing your entrails to ashes and your limbs to utter ruin. The arduous labor of a millennium will then have been made completely superfluous. After another five hundred years the calamity of wind will be sent to blow at you. It is not the wind from the north, south, east, or west; nor is it one of the winds of four seasons; nor is it the wind of flowers, willows, pines, and bamboos. It is called the Mighty Wind, and it enters from the top of the skull into the body, passes through the midriff, and penetrates the nine apertures.12 The bones and the flesh will be dissolved and the body itself will disintegrate. You must therefore avoid all three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, his hairs stood on end, and, kowtowing reverently, he said, “I beg the master to be merciful and impart to me the method to avoid the three calamities. To the very end, I shall never forget your gracious favor.” The Patriarch said, “It is not, in fact, difficult, except that I cannot teach you because you are somewhat different from other people.” “I have a round head pointing to Heaven,” said Wukong, “and square feet walking on Earth. Similarly, I have nine apertures and four limbs, entrails and cavities. In what way am I different from other people?” The Patriarch said, “Though you resemble a man, you have much less jowl.” The monkey, you see, has an angular face with hollow cheeks and a pointed mouth. Stretching his hand to feel himself, Wukong laughed and said, “The master does not know how to balance matters! Though I have much less jowl than human beings, I have my pouch, which may certainly be considered a compensation.” “Very well, then,” said the Patriarch, “what method of escape would you like to learn? There is the Art of the Heavenly Ladle, which numbers thirty-six transformations, and there is the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which numbers seventy-two transformations.” Wukong said, “Your pupil is always eager to catch more fishes, so I’ll learn the Art of the Earthly Multitude.” “In that case,” said the Patriarch, “come up here, and I’ll pass on the oral formulas to you.” He then whispered something into his ear, though we do not know what sort of wondrous secrets he spoke of. But this Monkey King was someone who, knowing one thing, could understand a hundred! He immediately learned the oral formulas and, after working at them and practicing them himself, he mastered all seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_2: The Seeker of Secrets, having learnt the three secrets of Immortality: mind and spirit and abstinence from sex, memorized these carefully, and went on studying alone for three years more. Then the Master again mounted the platform and preached on the Parable of the Great Judgment. Suddenly he asked, “Where is the Seeker of Secrets?” The Monkey King came forward, knelt and said, “I am here.” The Master asked, “What have you been learning all this time?” “Your disciple has mastered the study of the spiritual nature.” The Master said, “Then you know the origin of things. But you must be careful of three great dangers.” The Seeker of Secrets, after pondering over this for a long time said, “I have constantly heard it said that when one has found Truth and Virtue, then one becomes an Immortal and no sickness can befall him; how then do you speak of dangers to be avoided?” The Master said, “What I teach you is not an ordinary doctrine, for it controls the forces of Heaven and Earth and the secrets of the sun, moon, and stars. When one has arrived at this stage, then one is superior to the evil spirits and the ordinary gods. Still after a time there will come a thunderclap to try your soul and spirit. If unmoved and unshaken in the deluge, you will be like Heaven itself. If you doubt, then you perish. After a long practice of religion again, one is tried a second time. This danger does not come from Heaven, nor from man, but from one’s own passions. It burns one’s whole body to ashes, and all one’s long years of practice are in vain like a dream. After another long term of practice, one is tried a third time by the danger of environment, which blows on one like a typhoon and affects one’s whole being. This must be overcome.” When the Seeker of Secrets heard this his body shook and his hair stood on end. “Oh Master, have pity on me, and tell me how to overcome these three dangers, and I shall never forget your kindness.” The Master said, “That is not difficult. There are two ways to avoid them. One has 36 wonders, the other 72; which do you wish to know?” The Seeker of Secrets said, “I wish to know the 72 wonders.” “Come here then, and I will teach you the incantation.” Then he whispered it in his ear. The Monkey King felt influences going through every pore of his body, and began to practice the arts and to learn the whole 72 wonders.
human_translations.translator_3: Another three years passed before Subodhi reappeared to teach his disciples. He spoke of academic debates and parables and of external self-cultivation. “Where’s Monkey?” he suddenly asked. Monkey kneeled before him. “Here I am!” “What have you been working on of late?” “The basics of immortality: the nature and origins of all things.” “In that case, you have already penetrated the divine substance of matter. But beware of the peril of the three calamities.” Monkey mulled this over for a while. “Master is surely mistaken,” he eventually responded. “I thought that anyone who has learned the Way and is rich in virtue will live as long as Heaven itself. Neither fire, nor water, nor illness can harm him. What three calamities do you speak of?” “What you have learned is not ordinary magic. You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. translation: Three years had passed, the Patriarch ascended to the throne again and preached to the assembly. His teaching focused on subtle affairs, analyzing the external appearance and inner reality. Suddenly, he asked, "Where is the Monkey King?" The Monkey King approached, bowing down: "Your disciple is here." The Patriarch asked, "What has your disciple been cultivating these days?" The Monkey King replied, "I have recently gained a deep understanding of the law of nature and my root is gradually solidified." The Patriarch said, "If you understand the law of nature and have grasped the root, yet still have the Buddha-nature within you, you only need to be wary of the 'three disasters that bring harm'." The Monkey King listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words are wrong, venerable master. I often hear that a being with great virtue is long-lived and shares the lifespan of heaven, that water and fire are harmonized, and that all illnesses do not occur. How can there be the three disasters that bring harm?" The Patriarch said, "This is an extraordinary way: by depriving heaven and earth of their creative power, and invading the mysterious mechanism of the sun and the moon; after achieving the elixir, even the spirits find it hard to bear. Although you may remain youthful and long-lived, five hundred years will pass and heaven will send a calamity of thunder to strike you. You must first realize your true nature and be aware of your mind. If you can avoid it, your lifespan will be equal to heaven's, but if you cannot, you will meet your demise. Five hundred years later, heaven will send a fire that is not the fire of heaven nor the ordinary fire, known as the 'yin fire'. This fire will burn from the Cave of the Three Caverns and pass through the Palace of Dirt, turning the five viscera to ashes and reducing the four limbs to dust. Your thousand-year ascetic practice will all be illusions. Another five hundred years will pass and heaven will send a calamity of wind that is not the east, south, west, or north wind, nor the gentle breeze or the spring breeze, known as the 'absorbing wind'. This wind will blow into the cranial cavity and pass through the six orifices, then pierce the Dan field and the nine apertures, dissolving bone and flesh. That is why you must avoid them." The Monkey King heard this and his bones turned cold with fear. He bowed his head and said, "Grand Master, in compassion, teach me the method to avoid the three disasters." The Patriarch said, "This is not difficult, but because you are different from others, I am not permitted to teach you." The Monkey King said, "I also have a head that touches the sky and feet that stand on the ground, just like ordinary people, with nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six bowels. How am I different from others?" The Patriarch said, "Although you look like a human, you have fewer cheeks." The Monkey King indeed had a cheekless face and a pointed chin. He stretched out his hand to touch his face and laughed, saying, "Venerable master, you are mistaken! Although I have fewer cheeks, I have more of this pouch on my cheek, and it is enough to block the changes." The Patriarch said, "Fine, what will you learn from the ordinary world? There are thirty-six forms of the Heavenly Star, and seventy-two forms of the Earth Star." The Monkey King said, "I am willing to search through it all, let me just learn one form of the Earth Star." The Patriarch said, "Since you are determined, come forward and I will teach you the oral formula." He leaned in and whispered some mysterious method, and the Monkey King's one aperture was opened, at the same time understanding all hundred apertures. human_translations.translator_1: Three years went by swiftly, and the Patriarch again mounted his throne to lecture to the multitude. He discussed the scholastic deliberations and parables, and he discoursed on the integument of external conduct. Suddenly he asked, “Where’s Wukong?” Wukong drew near and knelt down. “Your pupil’s here,” he said. “What sort of art have you been practicing lately?” the Patriarch asked. “Recently,” Wukong said, “your pupil has begun to apprehend the nature of all things and my foundational knowledge has become firmly established.” “If you have penetrated to the dharma nature to apprehend the origin,” said the Patriarch, “you have, in fact, entered into the divine substance. You need, however, to guard against the danger of three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, he thought for a long time and said, “The words of the master must be erroneous. I have frequently heard that when one is learned in the Way and excels in virtue, he will enjoy the same age as Heaven; fire and water cannot harm him and every kind of disease will vanish. How can there be this danger of three calamities?” “What you have learned,” said the Patriarch, “is no ordinary magic: you have stolen the creative powers of Heaven and Earth and invaded the dark mysteries of the sun and moon. Your success in perfecting the elixir is something that the gods and the demons cannot countenance. Though your appearance will be preserved and your age lengthened, after five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of thunder to strike you. Hence you must be intelligent and wise enough to avoid it ahead of time. If you can escape it, your age will indeed equal that of Heaven; if not, your life will thus be finished. After another five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of fire to burn you. That fire is neither natural nor common fire; its name is the Fire of Yin, and it arises from within the soles of your feet to reach even the cavity of your heart, reducing your entrails to ashes and your limbs to utter ruin. The arduous labor of a millennium will then have been made completely superfluous. After another five hundred years the calamity of wind will be sent to blow at you. It is not the wind from the north, south, east, or west; nor is it one of the winds of four seasons; nor is it the wind of flowers, willows, pines, and bamboos. It is called the Mighty Wind, and it enters from the top of the skull into the body, passes through the midriff, and penetrates the nine apertures.12 The bones and the flesh will be dissolved and the body itself will disintegrate. You must therefore avoid all three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, his hairs stood on end, and, kowtowing reverently, he said, “I beg the master to be merciful and impart to me the method to avoid the three calamities. To the very end, I shall never forget your gracious favor.” The Patriarch said, “It is not, in fact, difficult, except that I cannot teach you because you are somewhat different from other people.” “I have a round head pointing to Heaven,” said Wukong, “and square feet walking on Earth. Similarly, I have nine apertures and four limbs, entrails and cavities. In what way am I different from other people?” The Patriarch said, “Though you resemble a man, you have much less jowl.” The monkey, you see, has an angular face with hollow cheeks and a pointed mouth. Stretching his hand to feel himself, Wukong laughed and said, “The master does not know how to balance matters! Though I have much less jowl than human beings, I have my pouch, which may certainly be considered a compensation.” “Very well, then,” said the Patriarch, “what method of escape would you like to learn? There is the Art of the Heavenly Ladle, which numbers thirty-six transformations, and there is the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which numbers seventy-two transformations.” Wukong said, “Your pupil is always eager to catch more fishes, so I’ll learn the Art of the Earthly Multitude.” “In that case,” said the Patriarch, “come up here, and I’ll pass on the oral formulas to you.” He then whispered something into his ear, though we do not know what sort of wondrous secrets he spoke of. But this Monkey King was someone who, knowing one thing, could understand a hundred! He immediately learned the oral formulas and, after working at them and practicing them himself, he mastered all seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_2: The Seeker of Secrets, having learnt the three secrets of Immortality: mind and spirit and abstinence from sex, memorized these carefully, and went on studying alone for three years more. Then the Master again mounted the platform and preached on the Parable of the Great Judgment. Suddenly he asked, “Where is the Seeker of Secrets?” The Monkey King came forward, knelt and said, “I am here.” The Master asked, “What have you been learning all this time?” “Your disciple has mastered the study of the spiritual nature.” The Master said, “Then you know the origin of things. But you must be careful of three great dangers.” The Seeker of Secrets, after pondering over this for a long time said, “I have constantly heard it said that when one has found Truth and Virtue, then one becomes an Immortal and no sickness can befall him; how then do you speak of dangers to be avoided?” The Master said, “What I teach you is not an ordinary doctrine, for it controls the forces of Heaven and Earth and the secrets of the sun, moon, and stars. When one has arrived at this stage, then one is superior to the evil spirits and the ordinary gods. Still after a time there will come a thunderclap to try your soul and spirit. If unmoved and unshaken in the deluge, you will be like Heaven itself. If you doubt, then you perish. After a long practice of religion again, one is tried a second time. This danger does not come from Heaven, nor from man, but from one’s own passions. It burns one’s whole body to ashes, and all one’s long years of practice are in vain like a dream. After another long term of practice, one is tried a third time by the danger of environment, which blows on one like a typhoon and affects one’s whole being. This must be overcome.” When the Seeker of Secrets heard this his body shook and his hair stood on end. “Oh Master, have pity on me, and tell me how to overcome these three dangers, and I shall never forget your kindness.” The Master said, “That is not difficult. There are two ways to avoid them. One has 36 wonders, the other 72; which do you wish to know?” The Seeker of Secrets said, “I wish to know the 72 wonders.” “Come here then, and I will teach you the incantation.” Then he whispered it in his ear. The Monkey King felt influences going through every pore of his body, and began to practice the arts and to learn the whole 72 wonders.
human_translations.translator_3: Another three years passed before Subodhi reappeared to teach his disciples. He spoke of academic debates and parables and of external self-cultivation. “Where’s Monkey?” he suddenly asked. Monkey kneeled before him. “Here I am!” “What have you been working on of late?” “The basics of immortality: the nature and origins of all things.” “In that case, you have already penetrated the divine substance of matter. But beware of the peril of the three calamities.” Monkey mulled this over for a while. “Master is surely mistaken,” he eventually responded. “I thought that anyone who has learned the Way and is rich in virtue will live as long as Heaven itself. Neither fire, nor water, nor illness can harm him. What three calamities do you speak of?” “What you have learned is not ordinary magic. You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. It burns from the soles of your feet to the cavity of your heart. It will reduce your entrails to ashes and your limbs to ruins. Your millennium of hard work will then be as dust and nothingness. After another five hundred years, Heaven will set the calamity of wind onto you. This is no earthly wind. It enters through the fontanels, blows through the six internal organs, midriff, and nine orifices. Your flesh and bones will dissolve and your body will disintegrate. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. How am I unusual?” “You bear a superficial resemblance to humans, but your cheeks are abnormally flat.” (Monkeys have rather angular faces, with sunken cheeks and pointed muzzles.) Monkey patted his face combatively. “Appearances can be deceptive. My cheek pouches have storage capacity on the inside. I demand parity.” “Fair enough,” considered Subodhi. “Which escape do you want to learn? There’s the Art of the Big Dipper, which involves thirty-six transformations, or the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which involves seventy-two.” “The more the merrier,” considered Monkey. “I’ll take the second.” “Come over here, then, and I will tell you the formula.” No one knows what Subodhi whispered into Monkey’s ear. But our hero was someone who could learn a hundred things from a single explanation. He immediately memorized the magic and, after practicing on his own, mastered the seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_4: After three years had passed in this way the Patriarch once more sat on his lecturing throne and expounded the Dharma to the students. He recounted famous sayings and parables, and discussed external phenomena and external appearances. Without warning he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong went forward, knelt down and replied, “Your disciple is present.” “What Way have you cultivated since coming here?” “Your disciple is now fairly well conversant with the Dharma,” Sun Wukong replied, “and my Source is getting gradually stronger.” “If you are conversant with the Dharma and you know about the Source,” the Patriarch replied, “and if the spirit has already flowed into you, then you must beware of the 'Three Disasters.'” Sun Wukong thought for a long time, then he said, “Patriarch, you're talking rubbish. I have often heard that the Way is lofty and its power mighty, that it is as eternal as Heaven, that it can overcome fire and water, and prevent all illnesses from arising, so how could there be “Three Disasters?'” To this the Patriarch replied, “This is not the ordinary Way: it involves seizing the very creation of Heaven and Earth, and encroaching on the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is made, devils and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it will preserve the youthfulness of your face and prolong your life, in five hundred years' time Heaven will strike you with a thunderbolt. You must be clear-sighted in nature and mind, so that you can hide from it before it comes. If you succeed in avoiding it you will live as long as Heaven; and if you don't, it will kill you. Another five hundred years later Heaven will burn you with fire. This fire will be not heavenly fire or ordinary fire but 'hidden fire'. It will burn you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head; your five viscera will be reduced to ashes, your four limbs will be destroyed, and a thousand years of asceticism will have been so much wasted time. Yet another five hundred years later a wind will blow at you. It will not be the North, South, East, or West wind, nor will it be a warm, fragrant wind from the Northwest; nor will it be the kind of wind that blows among flowers, willows, pine, and bamboo. It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation: But after three years had passed, the Venerable Master returned to his throne and taught the scriptures. His lecture was about analogies and cases, and he discussed the essence of one's external form. Suddenly he asked, "Where is the Monkey?" The Monkey drew near and bowed: "Your disciple is here." The Venerable Master said, "What practices have you been cultivating these days?" The Monkey replied, "Your disciple has recently achieved a certain degree of attainment in the Way and has gradually solidified his foundation." The Venerable Master said, "You have achieved the Way and have understood the root, yet your essence still contains the potential for three disasters." The Monkey listened and pondered for a long time before saying, "Your words, Master, are at fault. I've heard it said that one's virtue should be cultivated to the point where it equals that of Heaven, and one's lifespan should be equal to the heavens. When water and fire have reached harmony, one should not be susceptible to any illness. How can there be three disasters?" The Venerable Master said, "This is a transcendent practice: by usurping the creative power of Heaven and Earth, one invades the subtle principle of the sun and moon. Even though one may achieve a physical transformation and prolong one's lifespan, if one does not perceive one's true nature and avoid the disasters, one will be struck by a bolt of thunder after five hundred years and die. To avoid it, one must see through one's true nature and flee beforehand. If one can avoid it, one's lifespan will be equal to that of Heaven. If one cannot avoid it, one will die then and there. Five hundred years later, a disaster of fire will descend upon you. This fire is not the ordinary fire, but is called 'yin fire.' It will arise from your dantian and penetrate through to the crown of your head, reducing your flesh and bones to ashes and turning a thousand years of cultivation into an illusion. Another five hundred years later, a wind disaster will blow you away. This wind is not an ordinary wind, but is called 'ascended wind.' It will blow in through your fontanelle, pass through your dantian, and pierce through your nine orifices, causing your body to disintegrate and your flesh and bones to scatter. That's why you must avoid it." The Monkey listened and was deeply frightened, bowing his head in reverence and saying, "The Venerable Master is compassionate and has taught me how to avoid the three disasters. I will never forget your kindness." The Venerable Master said, "It is not difficult, but you are different from others, so it cannot be taught to you." The Monkey said, "I have a round head that touches the heavens and feet that stand firmly on the earth, just like other people. I have nine orifices, four limbs, five viscera, and six bowels, so how am I different from them?" The Venerable Master said, "You may look like other people, but you have fewer facial muscles." Indeed, the Monkey had a distorted face and a pointed chin. The Monkey reached out and touched his face, laughing and saying, "Master, you were mistaken! Although I have fewer facial muscles, I have a longer muzzle, which is just as good." The Venerable Master said, "Fine, you want to learn how to be like other people? You need to master the 36 transformations of the heavenly general and the 72 transformations of the earthly spirits." The Monkey said, "I wish to learn the 72 transformations of the earthly spirits." The Venerable Master said, "Since you are so determined, come closer and I will teach you the incantation." He then leaned in close and whispered some mysterious techniques. At that time, the Monkey was one-eyed and his intelligence was boundless. He memorized the incantation and practiced it on his own, eventually mastering all 72 transformations.

human_translations.translator_1: Three years went by swiftly, and the Patriarch again mounted his throne to lecture to the multitude. He discussed the scholastic deliberations and parables, and he discoursed on the integument of external conduct. Suddenly he asked, “Where’s Wukong?” Wukong drew near and knelt down. “Your pupil’s here,” he said. “What sort of art have you been practicing lately?” the Patriarch asked. “Recently,” Wukong said, “your pupil has begun to apprehend the nature of all things and my foundational knowledge has become firmly established.” “If you have penetrated to the dharma nature to apprehend the origin,” said the Patriarch, “you have, in fact, entered into the divine substance. You need, however, to guard against the danger of three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, he thought for a long time and said, “The words of the master must be erroneous. I have frequently heard that when one is learned in the Way and excels in virtue, he will enjoy the same age as Heaven; fire and water cannot harm him and every kind of disease will vanish. How can there be this danger of three calamities?” “What you have learned,” said the Patriarch, “is no ordinary magic: you have stolen the creative powers of Heaven and Earth and invaded the dark mysteries of the sun and moon. Your success in perfecting the elixir is something that the gods and the demons cannot countenance. Though your appearance will be preserved and your age lengthened, after five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of thunder to strike you. Hence you must be intelligent and wise enough to avoid it ahead of time. If you can escape it, your age will indeed equal that of Heaven; if not, your life will thus be finished. After another five hundred years Heaven will send down the calamity of fire to burn you. That fire is neither natural nor common fire; its name is the Fire of Yin, and it arises from within the soles of your feet to reach even the cavity of your heart, reducing your entrails to ashes and your limbs to utter ruin. The arduous labor of a millennium will then have been made completely superfluous. After another five hundred years the calamity of wind will be sent to blow at you. It is not the wind from the north, south, east, or west; nor is it one of the winds of four seasons; nor is it the wind of flowers, willows, pines, and bamboos. It is called the Mighty Wind, and it enters from the top of the skull into the body, passes through the midriff, and penetrates the nine apertures.12 The bones and the flesh will be dissolved and the body itself will disintegrate. You must therefore avoid all three calamities.” When Wukong heard this, his hairs stood on end, and, kowtowing reverently, he said, “I beg the master to be merciful and impart to me the method to avoid the three calamities. To the very end, I shall never forget your gracious favor.” The Patriarch said, “It is not, in fact, difficult, except that I cannot teach you because you are somewhat different from other people.” “I have a round head pointing to Heaven,” said Wukong, “and square feet walking on Earth. Similarly, I have nine apertures and four limbs, entrails and cavities. In what way am I different from other people?” The Patriarch said, “Though you resemble a man, you have much less jowl.” The monkey, you see, has an angular face with hollow cheeks and a pointed mouth. Stretching his hand to feel himself, Wukong laughed and said, “The master does not know how to balance matters! Though I have much less jowl than human beings, I have my pouch, which may certainly be considered a compensation.” “Very well, then,” said the Patriarch, “what method of escape would you like to learn? There is the Art of the Heavenly Ladle, which numbers thirty-six transformations, and there is the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which numbers seventy-two transformations.” Wukong said, “Your pupil is always eager to catch more fishes, so I’ll learn the Art of the Earthly Multitude.” “In that case,” said the Patriarch, “come up here, and I’ll pass on the oral formulas to you.” He then whispered something into his ear, though we do not know what sort of wondrous secrets he spoke of. But this Monkey King was someone who, knowing one thing, could understand a hundred! He immediately learned the oral formulas and, after working at them and practicing them himself, he mastered all seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_2: The Seeker of Secrets, having learnt the three secrets of Immortality: mind and spirit and abstinence from sex, memorized these carefully, and went on studying alone for three years more. Then the Master again mounted the platform and preached on the Parable of the Great Judgment. Suddenly he asked, “Where is the Seeker of Secrets?” The Monkey King came forward, knelt and said, “I am here.” The Master asked, “What have you been learning all this time?” “Your disciple has mastered the study of the spiritual nature.” The Master said, “Then you know the origin of things. But you must be careful of three great dangers.” The Seeker of Secrets, after pondering over this for a long time said, “I have constantly heard it said that when one has found Truth and Virtue, then one becomes an Immortal and no sickness can befall him; how then do you speak of dangers to be avoided?” The Master said, “What I teach you is not an ordinary doctrine, for it controls the forces of Heaven and Earth and the secrets of the sun, moon, and stars. When one has arrived at this stage, then one is superior to the evil spirits and the ordinary gods. Still after a time there will come a thunderclap to try your soul and spirit. If unmoved and unshaken in the deluge, you will be like Heaven itself. If you doubt, then you perish. After a long practice of religion again, one is tried a second time. This danger does not come from Heaven, nor from man, but from one’s own passions. It burns one’s whole body to ashes, and all one’s long years of practice are in vain like a dream. After another long term of practice, one is tried a third time by the danger of environment, which blows on one like a typhoon and affects one’s whole being. This must be overcome.” When the Seeker of Secrets heard this his body shook and his hair stood on end. “Oh Master, have pity on me, and tell me how to overcome these three dangers, and I shall never forget your kindness.” The Master said, “That is not difficult. There are two ways to avoid them. One has 36 wonders, the other 72; which do you wish to know?” The Seeker of Secrets said, “I wish to know the 72 wonders.” “Come here then, and I will teach you the incantation.” Then he whispered it in his ear. The Monkey King felt influences going through every pore of his body, and began to practice the arts and to learn the whole 72 wonders.
human_translations.translator_3: Another three years passed before Subodhi reappeared to teach his disciples. He spoke of academic debates and parables and of external self-cultivation. “Where’s Monkey?” he suddenly asked. Monkey kneeled before him. “Here I am!” “What have you been working on of late?” “The basics of immortality: the nature and origins of all things.” “In that case, you have already penetrated the divine substance of matter. But beware of the peril of the three calamities.” Monkey mulled this over for a while. “Master is surely mistaken,” he eventually responded. “I thought that anyone who has learned the Way and is rich in virtue will live as long as Heaven itself. Neither fire, nor water, nor illness can harm him. What three calamities do you speak of?” “What you have learned is not ordinary magic. You have stolen the creative power of heaven and earth itself, and penetrated the dark formulae of the sun and the moon. Ghosts and spirits will seek to bring you down. Although you have extended your life, in five hundred years’ time Heaven will unleash the calamity of thunder at you. You must seek wisdom to prevent this peril. Succeed and you will live as long as Heaven itself. Fail and you will die. In another five hundred years, Heaven will rain the calamity of the cold, dark fire of yin. It burns from the soles of your feet to the cavity of your heart. It will reduce your entrails to ashes and your limbs to ruins. Your millennium of hard work will then be as dust and nothingness. After another five hundred years, Heaven will set the calamity of wind onto you. This is no earthly wind. It enters through the fontanels, blows through the six internal organs, midriff, and nine orifices. Your flesh and bones will dissolve and your body will disintegrate. You see, then, why I recommend avoiding these calamities.” Monkey’s fur stood on end. “Tell me how to escape these horrors!” “Normally, this would be perfectly simple. But as you are an unusual specimen, I fear I cannot teach you.” “I’ve a head at the top and feet at the bottom, nine apertures, four limbs, five viscera, and six internal organs. How am I unusual?” “You bear a superficial resemblance to humans, but your cheeks are abnormally flat.” (Monkeys have rather angular faces, with sunken cheeks and pointed muzzles.) Monkey patted his face combatively. “Appearances can be deceptive. My cheek pouches have storage capacity on the inside. I demand parity.” “Fair enough,” considered Subodhi. “Which escape do you want to learn? There’s the Art of the Big Dipper, which involves thirty-six transformations, or the Art of the Earthly Multitude, which involves seventy-two.” “The more the merrier,” considered Monkey. “I’ll take the second.” “Come over here, then, and I will tell you the formula.” No one knows what Subodhi whispered into Monkey’s ear. But our hero was someone who could learn a hundred things from a single explanation. He immediately memorized the magic and, after practicing on his own, mastered the seventy-two transformations.
human_translations.translator_4: After three years had passed in this way the Patriarch once more sat on his lecturing throne and expounded the Dharma to the students. He recounted famous sayings and parables, and discussed external phenomena and external appearances. Without warning he asked, “Where is Sun Wukong?” Sun Wukong went forward, knelt down and replied, “Your disciple is present.” “What Way have you cultivated since coming here?” “Your disciple is now fairly well conversant with the Dharma,” Sun Wukong replied, “and my Source is getting gradually stronger.” “If you are conversant with the Dharma and you know about the Source,” the Patriarch replied, “and if the spirit has already flowed into you, then you must beware of the 'Three Disasters.'” Sun Wukong thought for a long time, then he said, “Patriarch, you're talking rubbish. I have often heard that the Way is lofty and its power mighty, that it is as eternal as Heaven, that it can overcome fire and water, and prevent all illnesses from arising, so how could there be “Three Disasters?'” To this the Patriarch replied, “This is not the ordinary Way: it involves seizing the very creation of Heaven and Earth, and encroaching on the hidden workings of the sun and moon. Once the elixir is made, devils and spirits cannot tolerate it. Although it will preserve the youthfulness of your face and prolong your life, in five hundred years' time Heaven will strike you with a thunderbolt. You must be clear-sighted in nature and mind, so that you can hide from it before it comes. If you succeed in avoiding it you will live as long as Heaven; and if you don't, it will kill you. Another five hundred years later Heaven will burn you with fire. This fire will be not heavenly fire or ordinary fire but 'hidden fire'. It will burn you from the soles of your feet to the crown of your head; your five viscera will be reduced to ashes, your four limbs will be destroyed, and a thousand years of asceticism will have been so much wasted time. Yet another five hundred years later a wind will blow at you. It will not be the North, South, East, or West wind, nor will it be a warm, fragrant wind from the Northwest; nor will it be the kind of wind that blows among flowers, willows, pine, and bamboo. It will be what is called a 'monster wind'. It will blow through the crown of your head down into your six entrails. It will go through the Cinnabar Field below your navel and penetrate your nine orifices. Your flesh and your bones will be destroyed and your body will disintegrate. So you must avoid all three of these disasters.” When he heard this Sun Wukong's hair stood on end, and he kowtowed with the words, “I implore you, my lord, to show pity and teach me how to avoid these three disasters. If you do I will be grateful to you for ever.” “That would be easy,” the Patriarch replied, “but for the fact that you are different from other people—which means that I can't.” “I have a head that faces the sky and feet standing on earth,” said Sun Wukong. “I have nine orifices and four limbs, five viscera and six entrails. How am I different from anyone else?” “Although you are quite like other people, your cheeks are too small.” Now the Monkey had a funny face, with cheeks that caved inwards and a sharp chin. Sun Wukong felt it with his hand and replied with a laugh, “Master, you didn't take everything into account. Although I'm a bit short of jaw, I've got more dewlap than other people to make up for it.” “Very well then,” the Patriarch said, “which would you prefer to learn: the thirty-six heavenly transformations or the seventy-two earthly ones?” “Your disciple wants to get as much out of it as he can, so I would like to learn the seventy-two earthly ones.” “If that's what you want,” the Patriarch replied, “come here and I'll teach you the spells.” Thereupon he whispered into Sun Wukong's ear, and who knows what miraculous spells he taught him? The Monkey King was the sort of person who understands everything once he is told a tiny part, and he learned the spells on the spot. He practiced and trained until he had mastered all seventy-two transformations.

translation: "The assembly would convene as planned; only after my emissaries retrieve the Great Vehicle Sutra, shall I, in utmost sincerity, carry out a good deed." All the officials uniformly obeyed. At the time, within the temple, someone asked, "Who dares to carry out the emperor's intention and go up to the West to offer incense to the Buddha to seek the true scripture?" Before the question could be finished, a monk suddenly appeared beside them and, bowing to the emperor, said, "This humble monk is of no ability, and I wish to offer the service of a dog or a horse to assist the emperor in seeking the true scripture, and pray that the kingdom of our emperor may forever remain secure." The Tang emperor was overjoyed, walked forward, and grasped the monk's hand with his imperial hand, saying, "If the monk is capable of this loyalty and virtue, no distance is too far, no road too perilous, I am willing to enshrine you as my brother." Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor truly was a paragon of virtue, went to the temple and before the Buddha, bowed four times and called out, "Your Imperial Brother, Holy Monk." Xuanzang expressed heartfelt thanks, saying, "Your Majesty, this humble monk has no virtue or ability, yet has been blessed by the heavens to receive such grace and favor. When I depart, I shall with my life, toil and strive until I reach the West. If I do not reach the West, and do not obtain the true scripture, I dare not return to the country, lest I fall into the abyss of the hells forever." He then took incense at the Buddha's feet, vowing thus. The emperor was delighted and ordered his attendants to return, waiting for a propitious day to depart, and issued an edict sending him on his way, and so the imperial retinue dispersed.
source_text: “且收胜会，待我差人取得大乘经来，再秉丹诚，重修善果。”众官无不遵依。当时在寺中问曰：“谁肯领朕旨意，上西天拜佛求经？”问不了，旁边闪过法师，帝前施礼道：“贫僧不才，愿效犬马之劳，与陛下求取真经，祈保我王江山永固。”唐王大喜，上前将御手扶起道：“法师果能尽此忠贤，不怕程途遥远，跋涉山川，朕情愿与你拜为兄弟。”玄奘顿首谢恩。唐王果是十分贤德，就去那寺里佛前，与玄奘拜了四拜，口称“御弟圣僧”。玄奘感谢不尽道：“陛下，贫僧有何德何能，敢蒙天恩眷顾如此？我这一去，定要捐躯努力，直至西天。如不到西天，不得真经，即死也不敢回国，永堕沉沦地狱。”随在佛前拈香，以此为誓。唐王甚喜，即命回銮，待选良利日辰，发牒出行，遂此驾回各散。
gt_translation: "Let's end the victory meeting, wait until I send someone to obtain the Mahayana Sutra, and then I will be honest and re-cultivate the good fruits." All the officials obeyed. At that time, I asked in the temple, "Who is willing to follow my will and go to the west to worship Buddha and seek scriptures?" I couldn't ask, but a Dharma master flashed by, and the emperor saluted and said: "The poor monk is not talented, I would like to do the hard work of dogs and horses, and seek truth with Your Majesty. The scriptures, pray to keep my king Jiangshan forever." Tang Wang was overjoyed, and he stepped forward and lifted his hand up and said: "The Master can do this loyal and virtuous, not afraid of the long journey, trekking mountains and rivers, I would rather worship you as a brother." Xuan Zang thanked him. Tang Wangguo was very virtuous, so he went to the temple in front of the Buddha, and worshipped Xuanzang four times, and he was called "the royal brother and holy monk". Xuanzang thanked him endlessly and said, "Your Majesty, what kind of virtue and ability does a poor monk have, and dare to be favored by the heavens like this? When I go, I must sacrifice my life and work hard until I reach the Western Heaven. If you dare to go back to your country, you will fall into hell forever." He sipped incense in front of the Buddha, taking this as an oath. Tang Wang was very happy, so he ordered him to return to Luang, waiting for a good day to be selected, and issued an ultimatum to go out, so he drove back to the various places.

human_translations.translator_1: We shall then renew our sincere effort to cultivate the fruits of virtue.” Not one of the officials disagreed with the emperor, who then asked in the temple, “Who is willing to accept our commission to seek scriptures from Buddha in the Western Heaven?” Hardly had he finished speaking when the Master of the Law stepped from the side and saluted him, saying, “Though your poor monk has no talents, he is ready to perform the service of a dog and a horse. I shall seek these true scriptures on behalf of Your Majesty, that the empire of our king may be firm and everlasting.” Highly pleased, the Tang emperor went forward to raise up the monk with his royal hands, saying, “If the Master is willing to express his loyalty this way, undaunted by the great distance or by the journey over mountains and streams, we are willing to become bond brothers with you.” Xuanzang touched his forehead to the ground to express his gratitude. Being indeed a righteous man, the Tang emperor went at once before Buddha’s image in the temple and bowed to Xuanzang four times, addressing him as “our brother and holy monk.” Deeply moved, Xuanzang said, “Your Majesty, what ability and what virtue does your poor monk possess that he should merit such affection from your Heavenly Grace? I shall not spare myself in this journey, but I shall proceed with all diligence until I reach the Western Heaven. If I do not attain my goal, or the true scriptures, I shall not return to our land even if I have to die. I would rather fall into eternal perdition in Hell.” He thereupon lifted the incense before Buddha and made that his vow. Highly pleased, the Tang emperor ordered his carriage back to the palace to wait for the auspicious day and hour, when official documents could be issued for the journey to begin. And so the Throne withdrew as everyone dispersed.
human_translations.translator_2: The pilgrim was to be accompanied by his chief disciple, the Sun the Seeker of Emptiness, Zhu the Seeker of Strength, and Sha the Seeker of Purity. And so on and so on. On hearing this Sha the Monk could not wait any longer, but cried out, “Brother Sun, the Master has lost his felt bag and the emperor’s edict, and now I see you have them. Do not heed the Master’s behavior towards you. Come back and let us continue our journey for the Sacred Scriptures. But if you are unwilling to return, I beg of you a thousand times to let me have the bag with the emperor’s edict.” The false Sun laughed coldly and said, “Having read this edict, I will myself go to the West for the Sacred Scriptures and acquire merit and make a name for myself that shall never be forgotten.” Sha the Monk replied, “That is impossible! It was never said that a monkey was to procure the Scriptures. If the Master does not go with you, Buddha will not give you the Scriptures.” The impostor answered, “But I have provided myself with a duplicate Master.”
human_translations.translator_3: “Deepest thanks.” Tripitaka bowed to him. Boqin returned the bow and they went their separate ways. Tripitaka and his new, still naked disciple set off across the Mountain of Two Frontiers. Soon enough, yet another tiger presented itself, snarling and swishing its tail. Tripitaka—on horseback—cowered; Monkey, by contrast, was delighted: “ Don’t worry, Master. He’s just here to deliver some clothes.” He pulled the needle-shaped iron out of his ear: with one wave, it became a thick cudgel. “Time to give my precious a little exercise, after five hundred years’ rest.” He strode up to the tiger. “Where do you think you’re going?” While the tiger crouched, as if mesmerized, Monkey with one blow smashed its brains and teeth into a gory porridge. Tripitaka rolled off his horse in terror at Monkey’s deadly speed.
human_translations.translator_4: If anyone is willing to go for them, His reward will be a golden body.” When he had read these lines Taizong issued an order to the assembly of monks: “Suspend this service until we have sent someone to fetch the scriptures of the Great Vehicle, and then you shall once more strive sincerely to achieve good retribution.” The monks all obeyed his instructions. The Emperor then asked those present in the monastery, “Who is willing to accept our commission to go to the Western Heaven to visit the Buddha and fetch the scriptures?” Before he had finished his question, the Master of the Law came forward, bowed low in greeting, and said, “Although I am lacking in ability, I would like to offer my humble efforts to fetch the true scriptures for Your Majesty and thus ensure the eternal security of your empire.” The Tang Emperor, who was overjoyed to hear this, went forward to raise him to his feet. “Master,” he said, “if you are prepared to exert your loyalty and wisdom to the full, not fearing the length of the journey or the rivers and mountains you will have to cross, I shall make you my own sworn brother.” Xuanzang kowtowed to thank him. As the Tang Emperor was indeed a man of wisdom and virtue he went to a place before the Buddha in the monastery where he bowed to Xuanzang four times, calling him “younger brother” and “holy monk.” Xuanzang thanked him effusively. “Your Majesty,” he said, “I have no virtue or talent that fits me for the sacred honour of being treated as your kinsman. On this journey I shall give my all and go straight to the Western Heaven. If I fail to reach there or to obtain the true scriptures, then I shall not return to this country even in death, and shall fall for eternity into Hell.” He burned incense in front of the Buddha to mark this vow. The happy Emperor ordered his chariot to take him back to the palace; later on an auspicious day would be chosen on which Xuanzang would be given a passport and set out. With that he returned and everyone dispersed.

translation:
"The great assembly was convened, awaiting the arrival of the great sutra with the envoy. Then, following the imperial decree, all officials took it upon themselves to abide by it. Meanwhile, inside the temple, someone asked, 'Who is willing to execute the emperor's will, to ascend to the Western Heavens to seek the sutra?' Before the question could be completed, a monk rushed over and paid homage to the emperor, saying, 'I am but a humble monk, willing to take on the tasks of a dog or a horse, to accompany Your Majesty in seeking the true sutra, to pray for the perpetuation of the kingdom and the dynasty.' The king of Tang was greatly delighted and approached to help the monk up with his imperial hand, saying, 'If you can fulfill this noble intent, I shall not be afraid of the distant road, traversing mountains and rivers, and I wish to acknowledge you as my brother.' Xuanzang bowed in gratitude. 

The king of Tang truly was extremely virtuous, and he went to the temple in front of the Buddha, and bowed four times to Xuanzang, calling him 'the imperial brother sage-monk.' Xuanzang expressed his thanks without end, saying, 'Your Majesty, what virtue or abilities could I have, to be regarded with such imperial favor and benevolence? If I were to go, I would surely give up my life in my efforts, until I reach the Western Heavens. If I were to fail to reach the Western Heavens, and fail to obtain the true sutra, I dare not return to my country, and risk being trapped in the hells of endless suffering.' He took incense in front of the Buddha, vowing with it. The king of Tang was greatly delighted, and ordered them to return to the palace, to select a propitious day and hour, and to issue an imperial edict to send them out. Thus, the imperial entourage dispersed in all directions."

translation: "Gather your distinguished colleagues, wait for my messenger to obtain the sacred sutras from the West, and then carry out a thorough revision of the good deeds. All officials obey my instructions accordingly. At that time, when inquired by me in the temple, 'Who among you is willing to carry out my intentions and journey to the West to pray to the Buddha to obtain the sutras?' Nobody replied. Just as the inquiry was about to be dropped, a monk walked past and bowed before the emperor, saying, 'I am an unworthy monk, willing to exert myself like a horse or dog and accompany Your Majesty to seek the true sutras and pray for the perpetual stability of the kingdom.' The Tang emperor was overjoyed, approached him and took his hand, saying, 'This monk truly displays filial piety and loyalty, and is not afraid of a long journey or traversing mountains and rivers. I am willing to make him my brother.' Xuanzang bowed his head in gratitude. The Tang emperor was truly a wise and virtuous king and, together with Xuanzang, bowed to the Buddha four times, and addressed him as 'Holy Monk, imperial brother.' Xuanzang expressed his heartfelt gratitude, saying, 'Your Majesty, I have no virtues or abilities, how could I be so fortunate as to have Your Majesty bestow such benevolence upon me? I am going to the West, determined to sacrifice my life and body, and will not return unless I have obtained the true sutras. If I do not obtain them, I dare not return to the country, and will be forever damned to the hell of transmigration.' He then held incense in front of the Buddha, taking an oath in this manner. The Tang emperor was overjoyed, ordered him to return to the palace, and selected auspicious days and hours for the expedition. He then issued a decree, and the emperor's retinue dispersed to prepare for the journey."
source_text: “且收胜会，待我差人取得大乘经来，再秉丹诚，重修善果。”众官无不遵依。当时在寺中问曰：“谁肯领朕旨意，上西天拜佛求经？”问不了，旁边闪过法师，帝前施礼道：“贫僧不才，愿效犬马之劳，与陛下求取真经，祈保我王江山永固。”唐王大喜，上前将御手扶起道：“法师果能尽此忠贤，不怕程途遥远，跋涉山川，朕情愿与你拜为兄弟。”玄奘顿首谢恩。唐王果是十分贤德，就去那寺里佛前，与玄奘拜了四拜，口称“御弟圣僧”。玄奘感谢不尽道：“陛下，贫僧有何德何能，敢蒙天恩眷顾如此？我这一去，定要捐躯努力，直至西天。如不到西天，不得真经，即死也不敢回国，永堕沉沦地狱。”随在佛前拈香，以此为誓。唐王甚喜，即命回銮，待选良利日辰，发牒出行，遂此驾回各散。

If the Master does not go with you, Buddha will not give you the Scriptures.” The impostor answered, “But I have provided myself with a duplicate Master.”
human_translations.translator_3: “Deepest thanks.” Tripitaka bowed to him. Boqin returned the bow and they went their separate ways. Tripitaka and his new, still naked disciple set off across the Mountain of Two Frontiers. Soon enough, yet another tiger presented itself, snarling and swishing its tail. Tripitaka—on horseback—cowered; Monkey, by contrast, was delighted: “ Don’t worry, Master. He’s just here to deliver some clothes.” He pulled the needle-shaped iron out of his ear: with one wave, it became a thick cudgel. “Time to give my precious a little exercise, after five hundred years’ rest.” He strode up to the tiger. “Where do you think you’re going?” While the tiger crouched, as if mesmerized, Monkey with one blow smashed its brains and teeth into a gory porridge. Tripitaka rolled off his horse in terror at Monkey’s deadly speed.
human_translations.translator_4: If anyone is willing to go for them, His reward will be a golden body.” When he had read these lines Taizong issued an order to the assembly of monks: “Suspend this service until we have sent someone to fetch the scriptures of the Great Vehicle, and then you shall once more strive sincerely to achieve good retribution.” The monks all obeyed his instructions. The Emperor then asked those present in the monastery, “Who is willing to accept our commission to go to the Western Heaven to visit the Buddha and fetch the scriptures?” Before he had finished his question, the Master of the Law came forward, bowed low in greeting, and said, “Although I am lacking in ability, I would like to offer my humble efforts to fetch the true scriptures for Your Majesty and thus ensure the eternal security of your empire.” The Tang Emperor, who was overjoyed to hear this, went forward to raise him to his feet. “Master,” he said, “if you are prepared to exert your loyalty and wisdom to the full, not fearing the length of the journey or the rivers and mountains you will have to cross, I shall make you my own sworn brother.” Xuanzang kowtowed to thank him. As the Tang Emperor was indeed a man of wisdom and virtue he went to a place before the Buddha in the monastery where he bowed to Xuanzang four times, calling him “younger brother” and “holy monk.” Xuanzang thanked him effusively. “Your Majesty,” he said, “I have no virtue or talent that fits me for the sacred honour of being treated as your kinsman. On this journey I shall give my all and go straight to the Western Heaven. If I fail to reach there or to obtain the true scriptures, then I shall not return to this country even in death, and shall fall for eternity into Hell.” He burned incense in front of the Buddha to mark this vow. The happy Emperor ordered his chariot to take him back to the palace; later on an auspicious day would be chosen on which Xuanzang would be given a passport and set out. With that he returned and everyone dispersed.

translation:
Carefree and easy, I drink and sing to my heart's content, and long songs and sighs follow the twists and turns of the wind. I invite my elder brother to join me, and call out to my younger brother to gather our boat companions. We bring our friends and acquaintances together to visit an elderly friend. We frequently play at guessing hands and exchange cups, we play cards and speak in riddles, and the sound of the drums resonates through the temple bell. We boil shrimp and steam crab every morning, and stir-fry duck and cook chicken every day. My foolish wife brews tea and scatters her emotions, while my mountain wife cooks with intention and composure. In the morning, I lift my staff and go fishing in the shallow waters, and when the day breaks, I carry firewood over the great slope. After the rain, I wear a cloak and catch the lively carp, and in the wind, I wield an axe to fell dry cedars. I hide my tracks and avoid the world, and don the mask of a fool. 

Zhang slightly said, "Li brother, I've taken the lead in starting a sentence. Now, brother, please compose a couplet to respond. And the younger brother should follow suit." "I am a wild man of the mountains and forests, under the influence of the moon and wind; I am a wandering vagabond of the rivers and lakes, and I take refuge in the leisure of an old pensioner. I have my share of leisure, and I spend it in carefree ease; I have no reputation or fame, and no noise or news comes to my ears. On moonlit nights, I sleep in a thatched hut; on cloudy days, my body is shaded by the water buffalo hat. I forget all cares and friendships with the friends I've made, and I delight in associating with herons and wild geese. I don't concern myself with profit or loss; I hear no sound of war drums or battle drums by my side. Whenever the mood strikes, I take a sip of fragrant wine; and I spend my days eating wild greens. Two bundles of firewood are my livelihood, and a fishing line is my means of sustenance. I call my young son to grind steel on the anvil, and quietly summon my simple-minded daughter to mend old cloth. When spring arrives, I enjoy seeing the green willows, and when the season is warm, I delight in seeing the emerald rushes. In the summer, I escape the heat to repair new bamboo; in June, I take a break from the heat by harvesting tender lotus roots. When the frost comes, I often cook chickens and slaughter crabs; on the Double Ninth Festival, I cook crabs that are strong and plentiful at the time. When winter arrives, I spend the day on the house, and in the ninth month, I do not have to worry about cooking.

translation:
I indulge in unrestrained singing, letting out carefree long songs, surrendering to the wind and rain. I call my friends and invite them to set sail, gather my colleagues and gather together in the countryside. We play the exchange-gift game and frequently pass the wine cups, discard the cards and casually gossip about the fortune-telling masters. We grill shrimp and boil crabs, singing and feasting every day, the foolish wife brews tea, and my wife prepares the meal with a composed mind. By daybreak, I lift my walking stick and fish in the shallow waters, by sunrise, I carry firewood and cross the great river. After the rain, I put on my hat and catch live fish, in the wind, I play with an axe, cutting down the dead pines. I keep a low profile, avoiding the world, pretending to be a fool. I hide my name and fade into obscurity, a deaf mute. 

Zhang asked, "Li Brother, I have just started a line, now I'll let my brother go first, little brother also has to continue." Li said, "A mountain man who fakes madness under the wind and moon, a rascal who registers as a retired veteran on the rivers and lakes. He is leisurely and free-spirited, with no trouble in his mouth, and his talk is always about enjoying a peaceful life. Under the moonlight, I sleep in a thatched hut, and when the sky is foggy, I cover myself with a reed mat. I've forgotten my desires and gotten to know my friends, the pine and the plum. I'm happy to form an alliance with the seagull and the heron. I don't care about fame or fortune, I don't hear the sound of armor and halberds. At any time, I take a cup of fragrant wine, and every day, I eat wild vegetable soup. The two bundles of firewood are my living, and the fishing line is my livelihood. At leisure, I call my young child to sharpen his axe, quietly I call my foolish child to mend his old fabric. When spring comes, I love to watch the green willows, and when the seasons blend, I enjoy watching the green reeds. In the summer, I avoid the heat and cultivate new bamboo, in June, I take a mid-day rest and pick the tender lotus roots. In autumn, I hunt and kill fat geese often, on the Double Ninth Festival, I boil the crabs in time. In winter, I go back to my room and sleep through the day, and in the ninth month, I stay up late, not even steaming rice.

translation:
To wander at will, and freely pour out one's passions, letting the wind blow and the world spin. I call out to my elder brother, and invite my friends to join me on a wild expedition. We take a boat, accompanied by fellow travelers, to gather wild mushrooms. We engage in rowdy games of chance, and exchange coins as we drink from the cup. We break open cards and announce each's fortunes, as they freely circulate around the clock. We grill shrimp and boil crab in the morning, and cook duck and chicken every day. My foolish wife brews tea and puts me in a lighthearted mood; my mountain wife carefully prepares meals with serene intentions. When morning comes, I take up my walking stick to wade through the waves; by day I carry firewood over the big hills. After the rain, I wear my raincoat and catch the living carp; before the wind, I hack at withered pines with my axe. I stealthily avoid the world, and wear a mask to conceal my foolishness; I hide my name and abandon my fame. 

Zhang Shi said, "Lee brother, I just came up with the first line, now it's your turn to come up with a pair, my little brother should also join in." Lee said, "The wild mountain man feigns madness under the wind and moon, the wandering merchant casts off the burden of age. I have leisure time, but I deliberately live carefree, and I disdain the quarrels that would bring me fame. At night I sleep in a thatched hut, my body wrapped in a reed mat. When the world is dark and the body is covered with a reed mat, I forget my worries and recall the friendships of a long time past. I enjoy meeting fellow travelers who share my love for the friendships of swans and herons. I don't calculate the value of fame or wealth, nor do I hear the sounds of war drums in my ears. Whenever I have a chance, I enjoy drinking fragrant wine, and live the simple life of eating wild vegetables for the three meals. My livelihood depends on two bundles of firewood, and my means of survival is one fishing line. In my leisure time, I call my little son to sharpen the steel axe; in my quiet moments, I call my foolish child to mend the old quilt. When spring arrives, I enjoy watching the green willows; when the seasons merge, I like to see the green stalks of the reeds. In the summer, I avoid the heat to plant new bamboo; in June, I use a fan to escape the heat and pick the tender lotus. After the frost comes, I enjoy eating roasting chicken daily; on the autumn equinox, I cook crabs at the right time. In the winter, I go back to sleep all day; by the ninth month, I am not steamed.

translation:
I play the flute freely, singing long songs and sighing carelessly, letting the winds and tempests blow. I call my brother over with a whistle, gather my companions and summon an old fellow to join us on the field. We order cups of ale and pass them around, our guesses flying like hands exchanging fortunes at the board of chance. We boil shrimp and steam crabs for our daily feasts, sauté ducks and roast chickens for our every meal. The foolish woman brews tea for us with a carefree heart, while the mountain wife cooks meals with an easy mind. When the morning comes, I take up my walking stick to fish for the gentle ripples, and when the day breaks, I carry a bundle of firewood to cross the big river. After the rain, I wear a waterproof mat and catch a living carp, and in front of the wind, I swing my axe to chop a withered pine. I hide my traces, withdraw from the world, and disguise my foolishness. I hide my name and conceal my identity, living a mute and deaf life. 

Zhang Zhongmou said, "Li brother, I'll start with a line, and now it's my brother's turn, and my younger brother should also follow suit." Li said, "The wild man in the mountains poses as crazy, and the old outcast enjoys the leisure of the winding streams. He has a share of leisure to idle about carefree, and no one spreads rumors about him with a tongue that longs for peace. Under the moonlit night, he sleeps in a grass hut securely, and when the heavens are dark, he covers himself lightly with a reed hat. He forgets his emotions and becomes friends with the fir and the plum blossoms, and he's happy to associate with the seagulls and the sandpipers in an oath of friendship. He doesn't count on fame or profit, and he doesn't hear the clanging of the spears in his ears. He drinks wine at any time and sips fragrant liquor, living from day to day on vegetable soup. He makes a living by selling two bundles of firewood and fishes with a single fishing rod. In leisure, he calls his little boy to grind steel axes, and in quiet, he summons his foolish child to mend his old clothes. When spring arrives, he likes to watch the green willows, and at the right time, he enjoys seeing the green reeds. When summer comes, he escapes the heat to fix new bamboo, and in June, he takes a siesta and picks the fresh water caltrops. When the frost arrives, he kills fat chickens every day, and on the Double Ninth Festival, he cooks the fresh crabs. When winter comes, he stays in bed all day, and when the ninth month arrives, he doesn't steam anything."

translation:
He sings, he toasts, and makes merry without a care, his long songs and sighs carried away by the wind. He calls his friend, invites his companion, and invites the villagers to gather together. The wine jar is passed and the cups are raised, the cards are shuffled and the dice are cast. Fresh shrimp and steamed crabs are savored daily, and stir-fried duck and roasted chicken are enjoyed every day. The foolish wife brews tea with a carefree heart, while the mountain wife cooks with a calm mind. When morning comes, he wields his staff to catch the morning waves, and at dawn he carries firewood over the great dam. After the rain, he dons a rain hat and catches a lively carp, and in the wind, he hews at a withered pine. He conceals his tracks and avoids the world, disguising himself as a fool.

Zhang Jian said: "Brother Li, I'll take the lead and start with a couplet; now it's my brother's turn to start a couplet, and the younger brother will follow suit."

"Wind and moon mock the rustic mountain man, the wanderer on the riverbank gazes at the retired old fellow. Leisurely he separates the fine from the coarse, carefree, he indulges in peace. At night, his body sleeps soundly in the thatched hut, and under the gloomy sky, his body is covered with a reed mat. He forgets the world and makes friends with pine and plum trees, and he's happy to form a bond with herons and egrets. He doesn't worry about reputation or wealth, and he doesn't hear the din of battle. He drinks a cup of fragrant liquor at will, and enjoys a simple meal of wild greens. Two bundles of firewood are his livelihood, and a fishing line is his daily occupation. When he's idle, he has his young boy sharpen his steel axe, and when quiet, he calls his foolish child to repair his old quilt. When spring arrives, he delights in watching the green willows, and in the warm breeze, he enjoys seeing the green lotus. When summer comes, he escapes the heat to plant new bamboo, and in the sixth month, he takes refuge in the cool shade to pick the tender lotus. When the frost descends, he often kills chickens at dawn, and on the Double Ninth, he cooks the fat crabs in time. When winter comes, he stays in bed all day, and by the ninth day of the ninth month, he cooks for himself without needing to be told."
