human_translations.translator_2: And to the tree of nature. Recognize no traitor as friend, Follow no artificial rules Lest you be deceived. Strike hard with your fist, But without malice. The apparent method is not real, The light of sun and of moon, Wherein lies their difference? Having traveled on, they came to a village where they sought lodgings, but the people were greatly frightened at the sight of Zhu Bajie with his long snout and flapping ears. So Sun advised him to hide his snout in his bosom and fasten his ears, to prevent them flapping. Food was served them, and the Master asked a blessing. Zhu Bajie ate ravenously. The host’s name was Wang and he said, “Before you there is a great mountain 800 li to cross. human_translations.translator_4: Singing and musing to myself I'm as wild as I care to be; Long songs, long sighs, I can let myself be crazy. As we play guess-fingers the cups fly fast; When we make riddles the goblets slowly circulate. Saute or boiled crab is a delight every morning; Plenty of fried duck and chicken cooked in ashes every day. As my simple wife brews tea, my spirits are untrammelled; While my mountain spouse cooks supper, my mind is at ease. At the coming of dawn I wash my stick in the ripples; When the sun rises I carry firewood across the road. I cover my tracks and hide from the world, acting the imbecile; I change my name and pretend to be deaf and dumb. “Brother Li,” said Zhang Shao. “I unfairly took the first lines just now, so now it's your turn to compose the first lines while I follow you.” Thus they continued: The man of the mountains acting mad under wind and moon; The haughty and unwanted dotard of the river. With his share of idleness, and able to be quite free; No sound from his voice as he revels in his peace. On moonlit nights he sleeps secure in a cottage of thatch; He lightly covers himself at dusk with clothes of reed. His passion spent, he befriends the pine and the plum; He is happy to be the companion of cormorant and gull. Fame and profit count for nothing in his mind; His ears have never heard the clash of arms. One is always pouring out fresh rice-wine, The other has wild vegetable soup with every meal. One makes a living with two bundles of firewood; The other supports himself with rod and line. One idly tells his innocent son to sharpen the axe of steel; The other quietly bids his slow-witted child to mend the nets. translation: The Russian heart can distinguish a great man even in the enemy of his homeland. That is to say, I don't remember if I literally expressed myself that way... I was a child, but I think that's what I meant! Napoleon was taken aback, he thought and said to his suite: "I love the pride of this child! But if all Russians think like this child, then..." – he didn't finish and entered the palace. I immediately intervened in the suite and ran after him. The suite parted to let me through and looked at me as a favorite. But all of that only flashed by... I remember only that, entering the first hall, the Emperor suddenly stopped in front of the portrait of Empress Catherine, looked at it thoughtfully for a long time, and finally said: "She was a great woman!" – and passed on. In two days, everyone already knew me in the palace and in the Kremlin, and they called me "le petit boyard". I only went home to sleep. At home, I almost went mad. Two days later, Napoleon's chamberlain, Baron de Bazancourt, who couldn't withstand the campaign, died. Napoleon remembered me; I was taken, led without explaining the matter, tried on the uniform of the deceased, a boy of twelve years old, and when I was brought to the Emperor in the uniform, he nodded at me with his head, and then announced to me that I was honored by his majesty's favor and was promoted to chamberlain of his majesty. I was happy, I indeed felt a warm sympathy for him... well, and apart from that, a brilliant uniform is a lot for a child... I went in a dark-green tailcoat, with long and narrow folds; gold buttons, red cuffs with gold embroidery, a high, standing, open collar with gold embroidery, embroidery on the folds; white striped breeches, a white silk waistcoat, silk stockings, shoes with buckles... and during the Emperor's horseback ride, and if I participated in the suite, high boots. Although the situation was not brilliant and the enormous misfortunes were already being foreseen, etiquette was observed as much as possible, and even more so, the more these misfortunes were foreseen.
source_text: «Русское сердце в состоянии даже в самом враге своего отечества отличить великого человека!». То есть, собственно, не помню, буквально ли я так выразился... я был ребенок... но смысл наверно был тот! Наполеон был поражен, он подумал и сказал своей свите: «Я люблю гордость этого ребенка! Но если все русские мыслят, как это дитя, то...» — он не договорил и вошел во дворец. Я тотчас же вмешался в свиту и побежал за ним. В свите уже расступались предо мной и смотрели на меня как на фаворита. Но всё это только мелькнуло... Помню только, что, войдя в первую залу, император вдруг остановился пред портретом императрицы Екатерины, долго, смотрел на него в задумчивости и наконец произнес: «Это была великая женщина!» — и прошел мимо. Чрез два дня меня все уже знали во дворце и в Кремле и звали «le petit boyard». Я только ночевать уходил домой. Дома чуть с ума не сошли. Еще чрез два дня умирает камер-паж Наполеона, барон де Базанкур, не вынесший похода. Наполеон вспомнил обо мне; меня взяли, привели, не объясняя дела, примерили на меня мундир покойного, мальчика лет двенадцати, и, когда уже привели меня в мундире к императору и он кивнул на меня головой, объявили мне, что я удостоен милостью и произведен в камер-пажи его величества. Я был рад, я действительно чувствовал к нему, и давно уже, горячую симпатию... ну, и кроме того, согласитесь, блестящий мундир, что для ребенка составляет многое... Я ходил в темно-зеленом фраке, с длинными и узкими фалдами; золотые пуговицы, красные опушки на рукавах с золотым шитьем, высокий, стоячий, открытый воротник, шитый золотом, шитье на фалдах; белые лосинные панталоны в обтяжку, белый шелковый жилет, шелковые чулки, башмаки с пряжками... а во время прогулок императора на коне, и если я участвовал в свите, высокие ботфорты. Хотя положение было не блестящее и предчувствовались уже огромные бедствия, но этикет соблюдался по возможности, и даже тем пунктуальнее, чем сильнее предчувствовались эти бедствия.

source_text: «Русское сердце в состоянии даже в самом враге своего отечества отличить великого человека!». То есть, собственно, не помню, буквально ли я так выразился... я был ребенок... но смысл наверно был тот! Наполеон был поражен, он подумал и сказал своей свите: «Я люблю гордость этого ребенка! Но если все русские мыслят, как это дитя, то...» — он не договорил и вошел во дворец. Я тотчас же вмешался в свиту и побежал за ним. В свите уже расступались предо мной и смотрели на меня как на фаворита. Но всё это только мелькнуло... Помню только, что, войдя в первую залу, император вдруг остановился пред портретом императрицы Екатерины, долго, смотрел на него в задумчивости и наконец произнес: «Это была великая женщина!» — и прошел мимо. Чрез два дня меня все уже знали во дворце и в Кремле и звали «le petit boyard». Я только ночевать уходил домой. Дома чуть с ума не сошли. Еще чрез два дня умирает камер-паж Наполеона, барон де Базанкур, не вынесший похода. Наполеон вспомнил обо мне; меня взяли, привели, не объясняя дела, примерили на меня мундир покойного, мальчика лет двенадцати, и, когда уже привели меня в мундире к императору и он кивнул на меня головой, объявили мне, что я удостоен милостью и произведен в камер-пажи его величества. Я был рад, я действительно чувствовал к нему, и давно уже, горячую симпатию... ну, и кроме того, согласитесь, блестящий мундир, что для ребенка составляет многое... Я ходил в темно-зеленом фраке, с длинными и узкими фалдами; золотые пуговицы, красные опушки на рукавах с золотым шитьем, высокий, стоячий, открытый воротник, шитый золотом, шитье на фалдах; белые лосинные панталоны в обтяжку, белый шелковый жилет, шелковые чулки, башмаки с пряжками... а во время прогулок императора на коне, и если я участвовал в свите, высокие ботфорты. Хотя положение было не блестящее и предчувствовались уже огромные бедствия, но этикет соблюдался по возможности, и даже тем пунктуальнее, чем сильнее предчувствовались эти бедствия.

translation: They had hardly reached the top when the painter tore the door open completely and, with a deep bow, invited K to enter. He refused to let any of the girls in, no matter how much they begged and how hard they tried to sneak in, either without or against his permission. Only the hunchbacked one managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around once, and then set her back down in front of the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had left his post, hadn't dared to cross the threshold. K didn't know how to assess the whole thing, as it seemed to be happening in a friendly agreement. The girls by the door stretched their necks one after the other, called out joking phrases to the painter that K couldn't understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchbacked one almost flew out of his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K, held out his hand, and introduced himself: "I am the artist Titorelli." K pointed to the door behind which the girls whispered and said, "It seems you're very popular in this house." "Oh, those creatures!" said the painter, futilely trying to fasten his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefoot and only wore a wide, yellowish linen pant that was secured by a strap whose long end swung back and forth. "These creatures are a true nuisance," he went on, abandoning the nightshirt whose last button had just come undone, fetching a chair, and forcing K to sit down. "I once painted one of them – she's not even here today – and since then they've been persecuting me. If I'm here myself, they only come in if I let them, but if I'm gone for even a moment, at least one of them is always here. They've even had a key to my door made and lend it to each other. One can hardly imagine how annoying it is. For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchbacked one at the little table, coloring her lips with a brush while her little siblings, whom she's in charge of, roam around and dirty up the room in every corner. Or, as it happened to me yesterday evening – excuse me, please, considering my state and the disorder in the room – I come home late at night and want to get into bed, and then something nips at my leg; I look under the bed and pull out another of those things. I don't know why they're pushing themselves on me; it's certainly not because I'm trying to lure them. You could probably notice that I'm not interested in them. This studio would be made available to me for free, and I would have moved out long ago if it weren't for it." Just then, a tiny voice whispered behind the door, "May we come in now?" "No," the painter replied. "Not even me?" asked the voice again. "Not me either," said the painter, went to the door, and locked it.
source_text: Sie waren aber noch nicht einmal hinaufgekommen, als oben der Maler die Tür gänzlich aufriß und mit einer tiefen Verbeugung K. einlud, einzutreten. Die Mädchen dagegen wehrte er ab, er wollte keine von ihnen einlassen, sosehr sie baten und sosehr sie versuchten, wenn schon nicht mit seiner Erlaubnis, so gegen seinen Willen einzudringen. Nur der Buckligen gelang es, unter seinem ausgestreckten Arm durchzuschlüpfen, aber der Maler jagte hinter ihr her, packte sie bei den Röcken, wirbelte sie einmal um sich herum und setzte sie dann vor die Tür bei den anderen Mädchen ab, die es, während der Maler seinen Posten verlassen hatte, doch nicht gewagt hatten, die Schwelle zu überschreiten. K. wußte nicht, wie er das Ganze beurteilen sollte, es hatte nämlich den Anschein, als ob alles in freundschaftlichem Einvernehmen geschehe. Die Mädchen bei der Tür streckten, eines hinter dem anderen, die Hälse in die Höhe, riefen dem Maler verschiedene scherzhaft gemeinte Worte zu, die K. nicht verstand, und auch der Maler lachte, während die Bucklige in seiner Hand fast flog. Dann schloß er die Tür, verbeugte sich nochmals vor K., reichte ihm die Hand und sagte, sich vorstellend: »Kunstmaler Titorelli.« K. zeigte auf die Tür, hinter der die Mädchen flüsterten, und sagte: »Sie scheinen im Hause sehr beliebt zu sein.« »Ach, die Fratzen!« sagte der Maler und suchte vergebens sein Nachthemd am Halse zuzuknöpfen. Er war im übrigen bloßfüßig und nur noch mit einer breiten, gelblichen Leinenhose bekleidet, die mit einem Riemen festgemacht war, dessen langes Ende frei hin und her schlug. »Diese Fratzen sind mir eine wahre Last«, fuhr er fort, während er vom Nachthemd, dessen letzter Knopf gerade abgerissen war, abließ, einen Sessel holte und K. zum Niedersetzen nötigte. »Ich habe eine von ihnen – sie ist heute nicht einmal dabei – einmal gemalt, und seitdem verfolgen mich alle. Wenn ich selbst hier bin, kommen sie nur herein, wenn ich es erlaube, bin ich aber einmal weg, dann ist immer zumindest eine da. Sie haben sich einen Schlüssel zu meiner Tür machen lassen, den sie untereinander verleihen. Man kann sich kaum vorstellen, wie lästig das ist. Ich komme zum Beispiel mit einer Dame, die ich malen soll, nach Hause, öffne die Tür mit meinem Schlüssel und finde etwa die Bucklige dort beim Tischchen, wie sie sich mit dem Pinsel die Lippen rot färbt, während ihre kleinen Geschwister, die sie zu beaufsichtigen hat, sich herumtreiben und das Zimmer in allen Ecken verunreinigen. Oder ich komme, wie es mir erst gestern geschehen ist, spätabends nach Hause – entschuldigen Sie, bitte, mit Rücksicht darauf meinen Zustand und die Unordnung im Zimmer –, also ich komme spätabends nach Hause und will ins Bett steigen, da zwickt mich etwas ins Bein, ich schaue unter das Bett und ziehe wieder so ein Ding heraus. Warum sie sich so zu mir drängen, weiß ich nicht, daß ich sie nicht zu mir zu locken suche, dürften Sie eben bemerkt haben. Natürlich bin ich dadurch auch in meiner Arbeit gestört. Wäre mir dieses Atelier nicht umsonst zur Verfügung gestellt, ich wäre schon längst ausgezogen.« Gerade rief hinter der Tür ein Stimmchen, zart und ängstlich: »Titorelli, dürfen wir schon kommen?« »Nein«, antwortete der Maler. »Ich allein auch nicht?« fragte es wieder. »Auch nicht«, sagte der Maler, ging zur Tür und sperrte sie ab.

The hunchback alone managed to slip in under his outstretched arm, but he rushed after her, seized her by the skirts, whirled her once round his head, and then set her down before the door among the other girls, who had not dared meanwhile, although he had quitted his post, to cross the threshold. K. did not know what to make of all this, for they seemed to be on the friendliest terms together. The girls outside the door, craning their necks behind one another, shouted various jocular remarks at the painter which K. did not understand, and the painter was laughing too as he almost hurled the hunchback through the air. Then he shut the door, bowed once more to K., held out his hand, and said in introduction: "I'm the painter Titorelli." K. pointed at the door, behind which the girls were whispering, and said: "You seem to be a great favorite here." translation: They hadn't even gotten up the stairs when the painter, from above, completely flung open the door and, with a deep bow, invited K. to enter. But he turned the girls away, even though they pleaded and tried to slip past him, even if not with his permission, then against his will. Only the hunchbacked one managed to slip under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, spun her around once, and then set her back down in front of the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had left his post, had not dared to cross the threshold. K. didn't know how to interpret the whole scene, it seemed to him as if everything was happening with friendly mutual understanding. The girls by the door raised their necks one after the other, calling out joking remarks to the painter that K. didn't understand, and the painter was laughing while the hunchback almost flew in his hand. Then he shut the door, bowed again to K., shook his hand, and introduced himself: "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering and said, "It seems they're very popular in the house." "Ach, the gnomes!" said the painter, and attempted, without success, to button up his nightshirt, which was hanging open around his neck. He was barefoot, and only wearing a broad, yellowish linen pant, tied to him by a long strap that swung freely back and forth. "These gnomes are a real burden," he continued, as he gave up on the nightshirt, which had just lost its last button, brought over a chair, and forced K. to sit down. "I once painted one of them - she's not here today - and since then, they've been chasing me. If I'm here myself, they only come in if I allow it, but if I'm away, then at least one of them is always here. They've made a key to my door and lend it to each other. One can hardly imagine how bothersome that is. I come home, for example, with a lady I'm supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find the hunchback at the little table, painting her lips red while her little siblings, whom she's in charge of, are running around, making a mess in every corner of the room. Or I come, like it happened to me yesterday, late at night - excuse me, please, out of consideration for my current state and the disorder in the room - I come home late at night and want to get into bed, something pokes me in the leg, I look under the bed and pull out another of these creatures. I don't know why they're pushing themselves on me, since I'm not trying to entice them. You would have noticed that too, I'm sure. Of course, I'm also being disturbed in my work. If this studio wasn't available to me free of charge, I would have moved out a long time ago." Just then, a small voice called from behind the door, "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," the painter replied. "I too?" the voice asked again. "No," the painter said, went to the door, and locked it.
source_text: Sie waren aber noch nicht einmal hinaufgekommen, als oben der Maler die Tür gänzlich aufriß und mit einer tiefen Verbeugung K. einlud, einzutreten. Die Mädchen dagegen wehrte er ab, er wollte keine von ihnen einlassen, sosehr sie baten und sosehr sie versuchten, wenn schon nicht mit seiner Erlaubnis, so gegen seinen Willen einzudringen. Nur der Buckligen gelang es, unter seinem ausgestreckten Arm durchzuschlüpfen, aber der Maler jagte hinter ihr her, packte sie bei den Röcken, wirbelte sie einmal um sich herum und setzte sie dann vor die Tür bei den anderen Mädchen ab, die es, während der Maler seinen Posten verlassen hatte, doch nicht gewagt hatten, die Schwelle zu überschreiten. K. wußte nicht, wie er das Ganze beurteilen sollte, es hatte nämlich den Anschein, als ob alles in freundschaftlichem Einvernehmen geschehe. Die Mädchen bei der Tür streckten, eines hinter dem anderen, die Hälse in die Höhe, riefen dem Maler verschiedene scherzhaft gemeinte Worte zu, die K. nicht verstand, und auch der Maler lachte, während die Bucklige in seiner Hand fast flog. Dann schloß er die Tür, verbeugte sich nochmals vor K., reichte ihm die Hand und sagte, sich vorstellend: »Kunstmaler Titorelli.« K. zeigte auf die Tür, hinter der die Mädchen flüsterten, und sagte: »Sie scheinen im Hause sehr beliebt zu sein.« »Ach, die Fratzen!« sagte der Maler und suchte vergebens sein Nachthemd am Halse zuzuknöpfen. Er war im übrigen bloßfüßig und nur noch mit einer breiten, gelblichen Leinenhose bekleidet, die mit einem Riemen festgemacht war, dessen langes Ende frei hin und her schlug. »Diese Fratzen sind mir eine wahre Last«, fuhr er fort, während er vom Nachthemd, dessen letzter Knopf gerade abgerissen war, abließ, einen Sessel holte und K. zum Niedersetzen nötigte. »Ich habe eine von ihnen – sie ist heute nicht einmal dabei – einmal gemalt, und seitdem verfolgen mich alle. Wenn ich selbst hier bin, kommen sie nur herein, wenn ich es erlaube, bin ich aber einmal weg, dann ist immer zumindest eine da. Sie haben sich einen Schlüssel zu meiner Tür machen lassen, den sie untereinander verleihen. Man kann sich kaum vorstellen, wie lästig das ist. Ich komme zum Beispiel mit einer Dame, die ich malen soll, nach Hause, öffne die Tür mit meinem Schlüssel und finde etwa die Bucklige dort beim Tischchen, wie sie sich mit dem Pinsel die Lippen rot färbt, während ihre kleinen Geschwister, die sie zu beaufsichtigen hat, sich herumtreiben und das Zimmer in allen Ecken verunreinigen. Oder ich komme, wie es mir erst gestern geschehen ist, spätabends nach Hause – entschuldigen Sie, bitte, mit Rücksicht darauf meinen Zustand und die Unordnung im Zimmer –, also ich komme spätabends nach Hause und will ins Bett steigen, da zwickt mich etwas ins Bein, ich schaue unter das Bett und ziehe wieder so ein Ding heraus. Warum sie sich so zu mir drängen, weiß ich nicht, daß ich sie nicht zu mir zu locken suche, dürften Sie eben bemerkt haben. Natürlich bin ich dadurch auch in meiner Arbeit gestört. Wäre mir dieses Atelier nicht umsonst zur Verfügung gestellt, ich wäre schon längst ausgezogen.« Gerade rief hinter der Tür ein Stimmchen, zart und ängstlich: »Titorelli, dürfen wir schon kommen?« »Nein«, antwortete der Maler. »Ich allein auch nicht?« fragte es wieder. »Auch nicht«, sagte der Maler, ging zur Tür und sperrte sie ab.

translation: They hadn't even reached the top when, above, the painter completely tore open the door and with a deep bow invited K. to enter. He, however, refused to let the girls in, as much as they begged and as much as they tried, if not with his permission, then against his will. Only the Hunchback managed to slip through under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, caught her by the skirt, whirled her once around himself, and then set her down in front of the door with the other girls, who, while the painter had left his post, had not dared to cross the threshold. K. didn't know how to judge the whole thing, for it seemed as if everything was happening in a friendly agreement. The girls by the door stretched their necks one after the other into the air, calling out various jocular meant words to the painter that K. didn't understand, and the painter also laughed, while the Hunchback almost flew from his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed again to K., offered him his hand, and introduced himself: "Kunstmaler Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls whispered and said, "It seems you're very popular in the house." "Ach, the Fratzens!" said the painter, futilely trying to fasten his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefoot and only wore a wide, yellowish linen shirt fastened with a strap whose long end swung back and forth. "These Fratzens are a true burden," he went on, abandoning the nightshirt whose last button had just come undone, fetching a chair, and forcing K. to sit down. "I painted one of them - she's not even here today - and since then, they've been pursuing me. If I'm here myself, they only come in if I allow them to, but if I'm away once, at least one of them is always there. They've had a key made to my door and lend it to each other. One can hardly imagine how troublesome this is. I come, for example, with a lady I'm supposed to paint, home, open the door with my key, and find the Hunchback there at the little table, dyeing her lips with the brush, while her little siblings, whom she's watching, are roaming around and making a mess in every corner of the room. Or I come, as it happened to me just yesterday, late at night - I apologize, considering your situation and the mess in the room - so I come late at night and want to go to bed, then something tickles my leg, I look under the bed and pull out another of those things. I don't know why they're pressing themselves on me, since I'm not trying to lure them to me, you might have noticed. Of course, this has also disturbed my work. If this studio hadn't been provided to me for free, I would have moved out long ago." Just then, a little voice whispered behind the door, timid and anxious: "Titorelli, can we come now?" "No," the painter answered. "I, either?" asked it again. "Not I," said the painter, went to the door and locked it.
source_text: Sie waren aber noch nicht einmal hinaufgekommen, als oben der Maler die Tür gänzlich aufriß und mit einer tiefen Verbeugung K. einlud, einzutreten. Die Mädchen dagegen wehrte er ab, er wollte keine von ihnen einlassen, sosehr sie baten und sosehr sie versuchten, wenn schon nicht mit seiner Erlaubnis, so gegen seinen Willen einzudringen. Nur der Buckligen gelang es, unter seinem ausgestreckten Arm durchzuschlüpfen, aber der Maler jagte hinter ihr her, packte sie bei den Röcken, wirbelte sie einmal um sich herum und setzte sie dann vor die Tür bei den anderen Mädchen ab, die es, während der Maler seinen Posten verlassen hatte, doch nicht gewagt hatten, die Schwelle zu überschreiten. K. wußte nicht, wie er das Ganze beurteilen sollte, es hatte nämlich den Anschein, als ob alles in freundschaftlichem Einvernehmen geschehe. Die Mädchen bei der Tür streckten, eines hinter dem anderen, die Hälse in die Höhe, riefen dem Maler verschiedene scherzhaft gemeinte Worte zu, die K. nicht verstand, und auch der Maler lachte, während die Bucklige in seiner Hand fast flog. Dann schloß er die Tür, verbeugte sich nochmals vor K., reichte ihm die Hand und sagte, sich vorstellend: »Kunstmaler Titorelli.« K. zeigte auf die Tür, hinter der die Mädchen flüsterten, und sagte: »Sie scheinen im Hause sehr beliebt zu sein.« »Ach, die Fratzen!« sagte der Maler und suchte vergebens sein Nachthemd am Halse zuzuknöpfen. Er war im übrigen bloßfüßig und nur noch mit einer breiten, gelblichen Leinenhose bekleidet, die mit einem Riemen festgemacht war, dessen langes Ende frei hin und her schlug. »Diese Fratzen sind mir eine wahre Last«, fuhr er fort, während er vom Nachthemd, dessen letzter Knopf gerade abgerissen war, abließ, einen Sessel holte und K. zum Niedersetzen nötigte. »Ich habe eine von ihnen – sie ist heute nicht einmal dabei – einmal gemalt, und seitdem verfolgen mich alle. Wenn ich selbst hier bin, kommen sie nur herein, wenn ich es erlaube, bin ich aber einmal weg, dann ist immer zumindest eine da. Sie haben sich einen Schlüssel zu meiner Tür machen lassen, den sie untereinander verleihen. Man kann sich kaum vorstellen, wie lästig das ist. Ich komme zum Beispiel mit einer Dame, die ich malen soll, nach Hause, öffne die Tür mit meinem Schlüssel und finde etwa die Bucklige dort beim Tischchen, wie sie sich mit dem Pinsel die Lippen rot färbt, während ihre kleinen Geschwister, die sie zu beaufsichtigen hat, sich herumtreiben und das Zimmer in allen Ecken verunreinigen. Oder ich komme, wie es mir erst gestern geschehen ist, spätabends nach Hause – entschuldigen Sie, bitte, mit Rücksicht darauf meinen Zustand und die Unordnung im Zimmer –, also ich komme spätabends nach Hause und will ins Bett steigen, da zwickt mich etwas ins Bein, ich schaue unter das Bett und ziehe wieder so ein Ding heraus. Warum sie sich so zu mir drängen, weiß ich nicht, daß ich sie nicht zu mir zu locken suche, dürften Sie eben bemerkt haben. Natürlich bin ich dadurch auch in meiner Arbeit gestört. Wäre mir dieses Atelier nicht umsonst zur Verfügung gestellt, ich wäre schon längst ausgezogen.« Gerade rief hinter der Tür ein Stimmchen, zart und ängstlich: »Titorelli, dürfen wir schon kommen?« »Nein«, antwortete der Maler. »Ich allein auch nicht?« fragte es wieder. »Auch nicht«, sagte der Maler, ging zur Tür und sperrte sie ab.

human_translations.translator_2: Yet they were still mounting toward the top when the painter flung the door wide open and with a deep bow invited K. to enter. As for the girls, he turned them off, he would not admit one of them, eagerly as they implored and hard as they tried to enter by force if not by permission. The hunchback alone managed to slip in under his outstretched arm, but he rushed after her, seized her by the skirts, whirled her once round his head, and then set her down before the door among the other girls, who had not dared meanwhile, although he had quitted his post, to cross the threshold. K. did not know what to make of all this, for they seemed to be on the friendliest terms together. The girls outside the door, craning their necks behind one another, shouted various jocular remarks at the painter which K. did not understand, and the painter was laughing too as he almost hurled the hunchback through the air. Then he shut the door, bowed once more to K., held out his hand, and said in introduction: "I'm the painter Titorelli." K. pointed at the door, behind which the girls were whispering, and said: "You seem to be a great favorite here." "Oh, those brats !" said the painter, trying unsuccessfully to button his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefooted and besides the nightshirt had on only a pair of wide-legged yellow linen trousers girt by a belt with a long end flapping to and fro. "Those brats are a real nuisance," he went on, while he desisted from fiddling with his nightshirt -- since the top button had just come off -- fetched a chair, and urged K. to sit down. " I painted one of them once -- not any of those you saw -- and since then they've all persecuted me. When I'm here myself they only come in if I let them, but whenever I go away there's always at least one of them here. They've had a key made for my door, and they lend it round. You can hardly imagine what a nuisance that is. For instance, if I bring a lady here whom I want to paint, I unlock the door with my own key and find, say, the hunchback over there at the table, reddening her lips with my paint brushes, while her little sisters, who she's supposed to keep an eye on, are scampering over the whole place and messing up every corner of the room. Or, and this actually happened last night, I come home very late -- by the way, that's why I'm in this state of disrepair, and the room too, please excuse it -- I come home late, then, and start climbing into bed and something catches me by the leg; I look under the bed and haul out another of these pests. Why they should make such a set at me I don't know, you must have noticed yourself that I don't exactly encourage them. And, of course, all this disturbs me in my work. If it hadn't been that I have free quarters in this studio I should have cleared out long ago." Just then a small voice piped behind the door with anxious cajolery: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," replied the painter. "Not even me? " the voice asked again. "Not even you," said the painter, and he went to the door and locked it.

Die Mädchen dagegen wehrte er ab, er wollte keine von ihnen einlassen, sosehr sie baten und sosehr sie versuchten, wenn schon nicht mit seiner Erlaubnis, so gegen seinen Willen einzudringen. Nur der Buckligen gelang es, unter seinem ausgestreckten Arm durchzuschlüpfen, aber der Maler jagte hinter ihr her, packte sie bei den Röcken, wirbelte sie einmal um sich herum und setzte sie dann vor die Tür bei den anderen Mädchen ab, die es, während der Maler seinen Posten verlassen hatte, doch nicht gewagt hatten, die Schwelle zu überschreiten. K. wußte nicht, wie er das Ganze beurteilen sollte, es hatte nämlich den Anschein, als ob alles in freundschaftlichem Einvernehmen geschehe. Die Mädchen bei der Tür streckten, eines hinter dem anderen, die Hälse in die Höhe, riefen dem Maler verschiedene scherzhaft gemeinte Worte zu, die K. nicht verstand, und auch der Maler lachte, während die Bucklige in seiner Hand fast flog. Dann schloß er die Tür, verbeugte sich nochmals vor K., reichte ihm die Hand und sagte, sich vorstellend: »Kunstmaler Titorelli.« K. zeigte auf die Tür, hinter der die Mädchen flüsterten, und sagte: »Sie scheinen im Hause sehr beliebt zu sein.« »Ach, die Fratzen!« sagte der Maler und suchte vergebens sein Nachthemd am Halse zuzuknöpfen. Er war im übrigen bloßfüßig und nur noch mit einer breiten, gelblichen Leinenhose bekleidet, die mit einem Riemen festgemacht war, dessen langes Ende frei hin und her schlug. »Diese Fratzen sind mir eine wahre Last«, fuhr er fort, während er vom Nachthemd, dessen letzter Knopf gerade abgerissen war, abließ, einen Sessel holte und K. zum Niedersetzen nötigte. »Ich habe eine von ihnen – sie ist heute nicht einmal dabei – einmal gemalt, und seitdem verfolgen mich alle. Wenn ich selbst hier bin, kommen sie nur herein, wenn ich es erlaube, bin ich aber einmal weg, dann ist immer zumindest eine da. Sie haben sich einen Schlüssel zu meiner Tür machen lassen, den sie untereinander verleihen. Man kann sich kaum vorstellen, wie lästig das ist. Ich komme zum Beispiel mit einer Dame, die ich malen soll, nach Hause, öffne die Tür mit meinem Schlüssel und finde etwa die Bucklige dort beim Tischchen, wie sie sich mit dem Pinsel die Lippen rot färbt, während ihre kleinen Geschwister, die sie zu beaufsichtigen hat, sich herumtreiben und das Zimmer in allen Ecken verunreinigen. Oder ich komme, wie es mir erst gestern geschehen ist, spätabends nach Hause – entschuldigen Sie, bitte, mit Rücksicht darauf meinen Zustand und die Unordnung im Zimmer –, also ich komme spätabends nach Hause und will ins Bett steigen, da zwickt mich etwas ins Bein, ich schaue unter das Bett und ziehe wieder so ein Ding heraus. Warum sie sich so zu mir drängen, weiß ich nicht, daß ich sie nicht zu mir zu locken suche, dürften Sie eben bemerkt haben. Natürlich bin ich dadurch auch in meiner Arbeit gestört. Wäre mir dieses Atelier nicht umsonst zur Verfügung gestellt, ich wäre schon längst ausgezogen.« Gerade rief hinter der Tür ein Stimmchen, zart und ängstlich: »Titorelli, dürfen wir schon kommen?« »Nein«, antwortete der Maler. »Ich allein auch nicht?« fragte es wieder. »Auch nicht«, sagte der Maler, ging zur Tür und sperrte sie ab.

human_translations.translator_1: They weren’t even all the way up yet, however, when the painter flung the door open wide and with a deep bow invited K. to enter. The girls, on the other hand, he fended off, he wouldn’t let a single one in, no matter how they begged, no matter how hard they tried to push their way in, if not with his permission, then against his will. Only the hunchback managed to slip under his outstretched arm, but the painter raced after her, seized her by the skirts, whirled her once around him, and then set her back down in front of the door with the other girls, who had not dared cross the threshold when the painter abandoned his post. K. didn’t know how to judge all this; it looked as if the whole thing was happening on friendly terms. The girls by the door craned their necks one after the other, called out various humorously intended remarks to the painter that K. couldn’t catch, and the painter laughed as well while the hunchback almost flew in his hands. Then he shut the door, bowed to K. again, held out his hand, and introduced himself: “I’m Titorelli, the artist.” K. pointed to the door, behind which the girls were whispering, and said: “You seem very popular here in the building.” “Oh those brats!” said the painter, and tried in vain to button his nightshirt around his neck. He was barefoot as well, and otherwise wore nothing but a pair of roomy yellow linen trousers, tied with a belt whose long end dangled loosely. “Those brats are a real burden to me,” he went on, giving up on his nightshirt, the last button of which had now come off, and fetching a chair, on which he made K. sit. “I painted one of them once—she isn’t even here today—and they’ve been pestering me ever since. If I’m here, they only come in when I let them, but if I go away, there’s always at least one of them here. They’ve had a key made to my door and lend it to each other. You can’t imagine how annoying that is. For instance I come home with a lady I’m supposed to paint, open the door with my key, and find let’s say the hunchback sitting at the little table there, painting her lips red with the brush, while her little sisters, the ones she’s supposed to be watching, wander around making a mess in every corner of the room. Or, as happened only yesterday, I come home late at night—in light of which I hope you’ll pardon my state and the disorder of the room —I come home late at night and start to get in bed when something pinches my leg; I look under the bed and pull out another one. Why they push themselves on me so I don’t know; you’ll have noticed yourself that I don’t try to lure them in. Of course they disturb my work too. If this atelier weren’t provided for me free, I would have moved out long ago.” Just then a small voice called from behind the door, softly and timidly: “Titorelli, can we come in yet?” “No,” answered the painter. “Not even just me?” it asked again. “Not even you,” said the painter, walking over to the door and locking it.
human_translations.translator_2: Yet they were still mounting toward the top when the painter flung the door wide open and with a deep bow invited K. to enter. As for the girls, he turned them off, he would not admit one of them, eagerly as they implored and hard as they tried to enter by force if not by permission. The hunchback alone managed to slip in under his outstretched arm, but he rushed after her, seized her by the skirts, whirled her once round his head, and then set her down before the door among the other girls, who had not dared meanwhile, although he had quitted his post, to cross the threshold. K. did not know what to make of all this, for they seemed to be on the friendliest terms together. The girls outside the door, craning their necks behind one another, shouted various jocular remarks at the painter which K. did not understand, and the painter was laughing too as he almost hurled the hunchback through the air. Then he shut the door, bowed once more to K., held out his hand, and said in introduction: "I'm the painter Titorelli." K. pointed at the door, behind which the girls were whispering, and said: "You seem to be a great favorite here." "Oh, those brats !" said the painter, trying unsuccessfully to button his nightshirt at the neck. He was barefooted and besides the nightshirt had on only a pair of wide-legged yellow linen trousers girt by a belt with a long end flapping to and fro. "Those brats are a real nuisance," he went on, while he desisted from fiddling with his nightshirt -- since the top button had just come off -- fetched a chair, and urged K. to sit down. " I painted one of them once -- not any of those you saw -- and since then they've all persecuted me. When I'm here myself they only come in if I let them, but whenever I go away there's always at least one of them here. They've had a key made for my door, and they lend it round. You can hardly imagine what a nuisance that is. For instance, if I bring a lady here whom I want to paint, I unlock the door with my own key and find, say, the hunchback over there at the table, reddening her lips with my paint brushes, while her little sisters, who she's supposed to keep an eye on, are scampering over the whole place and messing up every corner of the room. Or, and this actually happened last night, I come home very late -- by the way, that's why I'm in this state of disrepair, and the room too, please excuse it -- I come home late, then, and start climbing into bed and something catches me by the leg; I look under the bed and haul out another of these pests. Why they should make such a set at me I don't know, you must have noticed yourself that I don't exactly encourage them. And, of course, all this disturbs me in my work. If it hadn't been that I have free quarters in this studio I should have cleared out long ago." Just then a small voice piped behind the door with anxious cajolery: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," replied the painter. "Not even me? " the voice asked again. "Not even you," said the painter, and he went to the door and locked it.

translation:
They had not even gotten up the stairs when the painter ripped the door open wide and, with a deep bow, invited K. to come in. The girls, however, he waved away; he wouldn't let any of them in, no matter how much they begged and pleaded, not even against his will. Only the hunchbacked one managed to slip past him under his outstretched arm, but the painter chased after her, grabbed her by the skirts, whirled her around once, and then set her down before the door with the other girls, who, when the painter had left his post, had not dared to cross the threshold. K. didn't know how to make sense of the whole thing, for it seemed as if everything was happening in a spirit of friendly understanding.

The girls by the door stretched out their necks one after the other, calling out to the painter in a jocular tone things that K. didn't understand, and the painter laughed while the hunchback nearly flew out of his hand. Then he closed the door, bowed to K. once more, extended his hand, and introduced himself: "I'm painter Titorelli." K. pointed to the door behind which the girls were whispering and said, "It seems you're very popular in the house." "Ah, the faces!" said the painter, futilely trying to fasten the last button of his nightshirt, which had come undone. He was barefoot and only clad in a wide, yellowish linen shirt tied with a cord, the long end of which swung back and forth.

"These faces are a real burden," he continued, giving up on the nightshirt, fetching a chair and nudging K. to sit down. "I've painted one of them – she's not even here today – and since then they've been following me. If I'm here, they only come in if I let them, but as soon as I'm gone, at least one of them is always there. They've made a key to my door and lend it to each other. One can hardly imagine how annoying that is. For example, I come home with a lady I'm supposed to paint, unlock the door with my key, and find the hunchback sitting at the little table, lip-painting herself while her little siblings, whom she has to watch, run around the room and make a mess everywhere. Or, as happened to me yesterday evening – please, excuse my state and the mess in the room –, I come home late and want to go to bed, but something pokes me in the leg, I look under the bed and pull out another one of these things. I don't know why they're flocking to me, since I'm not trying to lure them over, as you might have noticed. That's also disrupting my work. If this atelier weren't provided for me free of charge, I would have moved out long ago."

Just then, a little voice called out from behind the door, soft and fearful: "Titorelli, can we come in now?" "No," the painter replied. "Not even just me?" asked it again. "No," said the painter, went to the door, and locked it.

translation: The evening was fresh, warm, and clear; the weather had been wild and untrammeled since morning. Raskolnikov was hurrying to his apartment; he was in a hurry to finish everything before sunset. As long as possible, he would not have wanted to encounter anyone. As he climbed up to his apartment, he noticed that Nastasya, torn away from the samovar, was intently watching him and following him with her eyes. "Is someone there?" he thought to himself. The image of Porfiry repelled him. But having reached his room and opened the door, he saw Dunya. She was sitting all alone, plunged in thought, and, it seemed, had been waiting for him for a long time. He stopped at the threshold. She leapt up from the sofa in fright and straightened up before him. Her gaze, fixed immobile on him, expressed horror and an unquenchable grief. And from this gaze alone, he already understood at once that she knew everything.
source_text: Вечер был свежий, теплый и ясный; погода разгулялась еще с утра. Раскольников шел в свою квартиру; он спешил. Ему хотелось кончить все до заката солнца. До тех же пор не хотелось бы с кем-нибудь повстречаться. Поднимаясь в свою квартиру, он заметил, что Настасья, оторвавшись от самовара, пристально следит за ним и провожает его глазами. «Уж нет ли кого у меня?» – подумал он. Ему с отвращением померещился Порфирий. Но, дойдя до своей комнаты и отворив ее, он увидел Дунечку. Она сидела одна-одинешенька, в глубоком раздумье и, кажется, давно уже ждала его. Он остановился на пороге. Она привстала с дивана в испуге и выпрямилась пред ним. Ее взгляд, неподвижно устремленный на него, изображал ужас и неутолимую скорбь. И по одному этому взгляду он уже понял сразу, что ей все известно.

source_text: Вечер был свежий, теплый и ясный; погода разгулялась еще с утра. Раскольников шел в свою квартиру; он спешил. Ему хотелось кончить все до заката солнца. До тех же пор не хотелось бы с кем-нибудь повстречаться. Поднимаясь в свою квартиру, он заметил, что Настасья, оторвавшись от самовара, пристально следит за ним и провожает его глазами. «Уж нет ли кого у меня?» – подумал он. Ему с отвращением померещился Порфирий. Но, дойдя до своей комнаты и отворив ее, он увидел Дунечку. Она сидела одна-одинешенька, в глубоком раздумье и, кажется, давно уже ждала его. Он остановился на пороге. Она привстала с дивана в испуге и выпрямилась пред ним. Ее взгляд, неподвижно устремленный на него, изображал ужас и неутолимую скорбь. И по одному этому взгляду он уже понял сразу, что ей все известно.
