Meanwhile the children were approaching by a long detour, for Peter knew many places where there were all kinds of good shrubs and bushes for his goats to gnaw on; therefore he made many turns on the way with his flock. At first the child had climbed in, panting in his heavy armor from the heat and discomfort and exhausting all his strength. He didn't say a word, but kept his eyes fixed on Peter, who jumped about effortlessly with his bare feet and light panties, and then on the goats, who with their thin, slender little legs climbed bushes and stones and steep slopes even more easily climbed up. Suddenly the child sat down on the floor, took off his shoes and stockings very quickly, stood up again, took off his thick red scarf, undid his skirt, took it off quickly and immediately had another one to crochet, because the Base Dete had put his Sunday dress over his everyday clothes, for the sake of brevity, so that nobody had to wear it. The everyday skirt was gone in a flash, and now the child was standing in a light petticoat, happily stretching his bare arms out of the short shirt sleeves into the air. Then she piled everything up nicely, and now she jumped and climbed after the goats and next to Peter, as easily as just one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid any attention to what the child was doing when it stayed behind. As soon as she jumped in the new clothes, he spread his whole face, grinning merrily, and looked back, and when he saw the little pile of clothes lying below, his face spread a little more, and his mouth almost came up to one ear on the other hand; but he said nothing. As soon as the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he also began to talk and had to answer many things, because the child wanted to know how many goats he had and where he was going with them and what he does where he goes. So at last the children, together with the goats, reached the hut upstairs and came face to face with Cousin Dete. But no sooner had she seen the company climbing up than she cried out loud: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? Where are your skirts and the second one and the scarf? And I bought you brand new shoes on the mountain and I made you new stockings and everything's gone! Everything's gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where's everything?"

human_translations.translator_1: Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the goats. As she could not find them anywhere, she climbed up a little higher to get a better view down the valley from there, and peered from side to side with marks of great impatience on her countenance. The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word. The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth. SHE UNDID THE HEAVY SHAWL AND THE TWO LITTLE DRESSES SHE UNDID THE HEAVY SHAWL AND THE TWO LITTLE DRESSESToList At last the children reached the summit in front of the hut. When Deta saw the little party of climbers she cried out shrilly: "Heidi, what have you done? What a sight you are! Where are your dresses and your shawl? Are the new shoes gone that I just bought for you, and the new stockings that I made myself? Where are they all, Heidi?"
human_translations.translator_2: For several minutes after Barbie had left her, Detie looked anxiously about for the two children with the goats, but there was no sign of them. She climbed a little farther up the path to get a better view and then stopped to look again. She was getting very impatient. The children had strayed far away from the path, for Peter always went his own way up the mountain. What mattered was where his goats would find the best bushes and shrubs to nibble. At first Heidi had scrambled up after him, puffing and panting, for her load of clothes made climbing hard, hot work. She did not complain, but she looked enviously at Peter, running about so freely on bare feet, in comfortable trousers; and at the goats whose nimble little legs carried them so lightly up the steep slopes and over bushes and stones. Then suddenly she sat down and pulled off her boots and stockings. She unwound the thick red scarf and quickly unbuttoned her best dress, which Detie had made her wear on top of her everyday one, to save carrying it. She took off both dresses and stood there in nothing but a little petticoat, waving her bare arms in the air with delight. Then she laid all the clothes together in a neat pile and danced off to catch up with Peter and the goats. He had not noticed what she was doing, and when he caught sight of her running towards him like that, he smiled broadly. He looked back and saw the pile of clothing she had left on the grass, and grinned from ear to ear, but he said nothing. Heidi felt much happier, and free as air, and began to chatter away, asking him a string of questions. He had to tell her how many goats he had, where he was taking them, and what he was going to do when he got there. Presently they reached the hut and came within Detie’s view. As soon as she spotted them she called out shrilly: ‘What on earth have you been doing, Heidi? What a sight you look! What have you done with your frocks? And the scarf? And those good new boots I bought you to come up here in, and the stockings I knitted for you? Wherever have you left them all?’ Heidi calmly pointed to the place where she had undressed.
human_translations.translator_3: Meanwhile Heidi and the goatherd were climbing up by a far and roundabout way, for Peter knew many spots where all kinds of good food, in the shape of shrubs and plants, grew for his goats. The child, exhausted with the heat and weight of her thick clothes, panted and struggled after him, at first with some difficulty. She said nothing, but her little eyes kept watching first Peter, as he sprang nimbly hither and thither on his bare feet, clad only in his short, light breeches, and then the slim-legged goats that went leaping over rocks and shrubs. All at once she sat down on the ground, and began pulling off her shoes and stockings. Then she unwound the hot red shawl and took off her frock. But there was still another to unfasten, for Dete had put the Sunday dress on over the everyday one, to save the trouble of carrying it. Quick as lightning the everyday frock followed the other, and now the child stood up, clad only in her light short-sleeved under garment. She stretched out her little bare arms with glee. Leaving all her clothes together in a tidy little heap, she went jumping and climbing up after Peter and the goats as nimbly as any of the party. Now that Heidi was able to move at her ease, she began to enter into conversation with Peter. She asked him how many goats he had, where he was going to with them, and what he had to do when he arrived there. At last, after some time, they came within view of Dete. Hardly had the latter caught sight of the little company climbing up towards her when she shrieked out: "Heidi, what have you been doing! What a sight you have made of yourself! And where are your two frocks and the red wrapper? And the new shoes I bought, and the new stockings I knitted for you—everything gone! not a thing left! What can you have been thinking of, Heidi; where are all your clothes?"

translation: The herdsman had likely waited for ten minutes and looked around in all directions to see if the children and the goats were nowhere to be seen; but as this was not the case, she climbed a little higher, from where she could see the entire alp down to the valley, and looked around from there with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile, the children approached on a large detour, for Peter knew several spots where the goats could find plenty of good leaves and bushes to eat; that's why he made the path to the mountain a winding one. At first, the child had climbed laboriously, panting in its heavy armor due to the heat and the discomfort, and exerting all its strength. It didn't say a word, but looked intently at Peter, who jumped back and forth with his bare feet and light pants without any effort, and at the goats that climbed up over bushes and stones and steep slopes with their thin, slender legs. At one point, the child sat down on the ground, quickly pulled off its shoes and stockings, stood up, pulled off its red, thick neck scarf, undid its little skirt, quickly took it off, and had to quickly knit another one, because Dete had put the Sunday dress over the everyday clothes so as not to have to wear it. Just as quickly, the everyday little skirt was gone, and now the child stood in the light underskirt, happily stretching its bare arms out of the short shirt sleeves. Then it neatly put everything into a little heap, and now it sprang and climbed behind the goats and next to Peter, as light as one of the whole society. Peter hadn't noticed what the child was doing as it lagged behind. As it sprang back, wearing the new clothes, he grinned happily and stretched his face wide open and looked back, and when he saw the little pile of clothes lying below, his face stretched even further apart, and his mouth almost from one ear to the other; he didn't say a word. When the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he started talking and had to answer many things because the child wanted to know how many goats he had and where he was going with them and what he would do when he got there. Finally, the children with the goats arrived at the hut and met Dete. As soon as this had caught sight of the approaching group, she loudly cried out: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? Where is your dress and the second one and the scarf? And I bought you new shoes for the mountain and made you new stockings, and all of it is gone! Everything is gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where have you done everything?"
source_text: Die Dete hatte wohl zehn Minuten gewartet und sich nach allen Seiten umgesehen, ob die Kinder mit den Geißen noch nirgends zu sehen seien; als dies aber nicht der Fall war, so stieg sie noch ein wenig höher, wo sie besser die ganze Alm bis hinunter übersehen konnte, und guckte nun von hier aus bald dahin, bald dorthin mit Zeichen großer Ungeduld auf dem Gesicht und in den Bewegungen. Unterdessen rückten die Kinder auf einem großen Umwege heran, denn der Peter wusste viele Stellen, wo allerhand Gutes an Sträuchern und Gebüschen für seine Geißen zu nagen war; darum machte er mit seiner Herde vielerlei Wendungen auf dem Wege. Erst war das Kind mühsam nachgeklettert, in seiner schweren Rüstung vor Hitze und Unbequemlichkeit keuchend und alle Kräfte anstrengend. Es sagte kein Wort, blickte aber unverwandt bald auf den Peter, der mit seinen nackten Füßen und leichten Höschen ohne alle Mühe hin und her sprang, bald auf die Geißen, die mit den dünnen, schlanken Beinchen noch leichter über Busch und Stein und steile Abhänge hinaufkletterten. Auf einmal setzte das Kind sich auf den Boden nieder, zog mit großer Schnelligkeit Schuhe und Strümpfe aus, stand wieder auf, zog sein rotes, dickes Halstuch weg, machte sein Röckchen auf, zog es schnell aus und hatte gleich noch eins auszuhäkeln, denn die Base Dete hatte ihm das Sonntagskleidchen über das Alltagszeug angezogen, um der Kürze willen, damit niemand es tragen müsse. Blitzschnell war auch das Alltagsröcklein weg, und nun stand das Kind im leichten Unterröckchen, die bloßen Arme aus den kurzen Hemdärmelchen vergnüglich in die Luft hinausstreckend. Dann legte es schön alles auf ein Häufchen, und nun sprang und kletterte es hinter den Geißen und neben dem Peter her, so leicht als nur eines aus der ganzen Gesellschaft. Der Peter hatte nicht Acht gegeben, was das Kind mache, als es zurückgeblieben war. Wie es nun in der neuen Bekleidung nachgesprungen kam, zog er lustig grinsend das ganze Gesicht auseinander und schaute zurück, und wie er unten das Häuflein Kleider liegen sah, ging sein Gesicht noch ein wenig mehr auseinander, und sein Mund kam fast von einem Ohr bis zum anderen; er sagte aber nichts. Wie nun das Kind sich so frei und leicht fühlte, fing es ein Gespräch mit dem Peter an, und er fing auch an zu reden und musste auf vielerlei antworten, denn das Kind wollte wissen, wie viele Geißen er habe und wohin er mit ihnen gehe und was er dort tue, wo er hinkomme. So langten endlich die Kinder samt den Geißen oben bei der Hütte an und kamen der Base Dete zu Gesicht. Kaum aber hatte diese die herankletternde Gesellschaft erblickt, als sie laut aufschrie: "Heidi, was machst du? Wie siehst du aus? Wo hast du deinen Rock und den zweiten und das Halstuch? Und ganz neue Schuhe habe ich dir gekauft auf den Berg und dir neue Strümpfe gemacht, und alles fort! Alles fort! Heidi, was machst du, wo hast du alles?"

human_translations.translator_1: Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the goats. As she could not find them anywhere, she climbed up a little higher to get a better view down the valley from there, and peered from side to side with marks of great impatience on her countenance. The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word. The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth. She said nothing, but her little eyes kept watching first Peter, as he sprang nimbly hither and thither on his bare feet, clad only in his short, light breeches, and then the slim-legged goats that went leaping over rocks and shrubs. All at once she sat down on the ground, and began pulling off her shoes and stockings. Then she unwound the hot red shawl and took off her frock. But there was still another to unfasten, for Dete had put the Sunday dress on over the everyday one, to save the trouble of carrying it. Quick as lightning the everyday frock followed the other, and now the child stood up, clad only in her light short-sleeved under garment. She stretched out her little bare arms with glee. Leaving all her clothes together in a tidy little heap, she went jumping and climbing up after Peter and the goats as nimbly as any of the party. Now that Heidi was able to move at her ease, she began to enter into conversation with Peter. She asked him how many goats he had, where he was going to with them, and what he had to do when he arrived there. At last, after some time, they came within view of Dete. Hardly had the latter caught sight of the little company climbing up towards her when she shrieked out: "Heidi, what have you been doing! What a sight you have made of yourself! And where are your two frocks and the red wrapper? And the new shoes I bought, and the new stockings I knitted for you—everything gone! not a thing left! What can you have been thinking of, Heidi; where are all your clothes?"

translation: The nurse had likely waited for ten minutes and looked all around to see if the children and the goats were nowhere to be seen; but as this was not the case, she climbed a little higher where she could see the whole alp down below better, and looked out this way and that way with signs of great impatience on her face and in her movements. Meanwhile, the children made their way up on a long detour, for Peter knew many places where there were plenty of good bushes and shrubs for his goats to graze on; that's why he made many turns on the path. First, the child had laboriously climbed up, panting and gasping in its heavy armor because of the heat and discomfort, and straining all its forces. It didn't say a word, but gazed steadfastly at Peter, who sprang about barefoot and in his light undershirt without any effort, or at the goats, which climbed with their thin, slender legs easily over bush and stone and steep slopes. Suddenly, the child sat down on the ground, quickly pulled off its shoes and stockings, stood up, pulled off its red, thick neck scarf, undid its dress, quickly took it off, and had to hem another one right away, because Nurse Dete had put the Sunday dress over the everyday clothes on the child for the sake of brevity, so that no one would have to wear it. Just as quickly, the everyday underskirt was gone, and now the child stood in its light underskirt, its bare arms stretching out of its short sleeves into the air with pleasure. Then it put all the clothes neatly in a pile, and now it sprang and climbed behind the goats and alongside Peter, as lightly as if it were one of the whole company. Peter hadn't paid attention to what the child was doing as it had been lagging behind. When it now came springing along in its new clothes, he grinned widely and pulled his whole face apart, looked back, and when he saw the pile of clothes lying below, his face stretched even further apart, and his mouth almost from ear to ear; but he didn't say a word. Now that the child felt so free and light, it started a conversation with Peter, and he started talking and had to answer many things, because the child wanted to know how many goats he had and where he was going and what he would do when he got there. Finally, the children with the goats arrived at the top of the hut and came face to face with Nurse Dete. Scarcely had she seen the approaching company when she let out a loud cry: "Heidi, what are you doing? How do you look? Where is your dress and the other one and the neck scarf? And I bought you new shoes for the mountain and made you new stockings, and everything's gone! Everything's gone! Heidi, what are you doing, where is everything?"
source_text: Die Dete hatte wohl zehn Minuten gewartet und sich nach allen Seiten umgesehen, ob die Kinder mit den Geißen noch nirgends zu sehen seien; als dies aber nicht der Fall war, so stieg sie noch ein wenig höher, wo sie besser die ganze Alm bis hinunter übersehen konnte, und guckte nun von hier aus bald dahin, bald dorthin mit Zeichen großer Ungeduld auf dem Gesicht und in den Bewegungen. Unterdessen rückten die Kinder auf einem großen Umwege heran, denn der Peter wusste viele Stellen, wo allerhand Gutes an Sträuchern und Gebüschen für seine Geißen zu nagen war; darum machte er mit seiner Herde vielerlei Wendungen auf dem Wege. Erst war das Kind mühsam nachgeklettert, in seiner schweren Rüstung vor Hitze und Unbequemlichkeit keuchend und alle Kräfte anstrengend. Es sagte kein Wort, blickte aber unverwandt bald auf den Peter, der mit seinen nackten Füßen und leichten Höschen ohne alle Mühe hin und her sprang, bald auf die Geißen, die mit den dünnen, schlanken Beinchen noch leichter über Busch und Stein und steile Abhänge hinaufkletterten. Auf einmal setzte das Kind sich auf den Boden nieder, zog mit großer Schnelligkeit Schuhe und Strümpfe aus, stand wieder auf, zog sein rotes, dickes Halstuch weg, machte sein Röckchen auf, zog es schnell aus und hatte gleich noch eins auszuhäkeln, denn die Base Dete hatte ihm das Sonntagskleidchen über das Alltagszeug angezogen, um der Kürze willen, damit niemand es tragen müsse. Blitzschnell war auch das Alltagsröcklein weg, und nun stand das Kind im leichten Unterröckchen, die bloßen Arme aus den kurzen Hemdärmelchen vergnüglich in die Luft hinausstreckend. Dann legte es schön alles auf ein Häufchen, und nun sprang und kletterte es hinter den Geißen und neben dem Peter her, so leicht als nur eines aus der ganzen Gesellschaft. Der Peter hatte nicht Acht gegeben, was das Kind mache, als es zurückgeblieben war. Wie es nun in der neuen Bekleidung nachgesprungen kam, zog er lustig grinsend das ganze Gesicht auseinander und schaute zurück, und wie er unten das Häuflein Kleider liegen sah, ging sein Gesicht noch ein wenig mehr auseinander, und sein Mund kam fast von einem Ohr bis zum anderen; er sagte aber nichts. Wie nun das Kind sich so frei und leicht fühlte, fing es ein Gespräch mit dem Peter an, und er fing auch an zu reden und musste auf vielerlei antworten, denn das Kind wollte wissen, wie viele Geißen er habe und wohin er mit ihnen gehe und was er dort tue, wo er hinkomme. So langten endlich die Kinder samt den Geißen oben bei der Hütte an und kamen der Base Dete zu Gesicht. Kaum aber hatte diese die herankletternde Gesellschaft erblickt, als sie laut aufschrie: "Heidi, was machst du? Wie siehst du aus? Wo hast du deinen Rock und den zweiten und das Halstuch? Und ganz neue Schuhe habe ich dir gekauft auf den Berg und dir neue Strümpfe gemacht, und alles fort! Alles fort! Heidi, was machst du, wo hast du alles?"

human_translations.translator_1: Deta waited about ten minutes to see if the children were coming up behind with the goats. As she could not find them anywhere, she climbed up a little higher to get a better view down the valley from there, and peered from side to side with marks of great impatience on her countenance. The children in the meantime were ascending slowly in a zigzag way, Peter always knowing where to find all sorts of good grazing places for his goats where they could nibble. Thus they strayed from side to side. The poor little girl had followed the boy only with the greatest effort and she was panting in her heavy clothes. She was so hot and uncomfortable that she only climbed by exerting all her strength. She did not say anything but looked enviously at Peter, who jumped about so easily in his light trousers and bare feet. She envied even more the goats that climbed over bushes, stones, and steep inclines with their slender legs. Suddenly sitting down on the ground the child swiftly took off her shoes and stockings. Getting up she undid the heavy shawl and the two little dresses. Out she slipped without more ado and stood up in only a light petticoat. In sheer delight at the relief, she threw up her dimpled arms, that were bare up to her short sleeves. To save the trouble of carrying them, her aunt had dressed her in her Sunday clothes over her workday garments. Heidi arranged her dresses neatly in a heap and joined Peter and the goats. She was now as light-footed as any of them. When Peter, who had not paid much attention, saw her suddenly in her light attire, he grinned. Looking back, he saw the little heap of dresses on the ground and then he grinned yet more, till his mouth seemed to reach from ear to ear; but he said never a word. The child, feeling free and comfortable, started to converse with Peter, and he had to answer many questions. She asked him how many goats he had, and where he led them, what he did with them when he got there, and so forth. human_translations.translator_2: For several minutes after Barbie had left her, Detie looked anxiously about for the two children with the goats, but there was no sign of them. She climbed a little farther up the path to get a better view and then stopped to look again. She was getting very impatient. The children had strayed far away from the path, for Peter always went his own way up the mountain. What mattered was where his goats would find the best bushes and shrubs to nibble. At first Heidi had scrambled up after him, puffing and panting, for her load of clothes made climbing hard, hot work. She did not complain, but she looked enviously at Peter, running about so freely on bare feet, in comfortable trousers; and at the goats whose nimble little legs carried them so lightly up the steep slopes and over bushes and stones. Then suddenly she sat down and pulled off her boots and stockings. She unwound the thick red scarf and quickly unbuttoned her best dress, which Detie had made her wear on top of her everyday one, to save carrying it. She took off both dresses and stood there in nothing but a little petticoat, waving her bare arms in the air with delight. Then she laid all the clothes together in a neat pile and danced off to catch up with Peter and the goats. He had not noticed what she was doing, and when he caught sight of her running towards him like that, he smiled broadly. He looked back and saw the pile of clothing she had left on the grass, and grinned from ear to ear, but he said nothing. Heidi felt much happier, and free as air, and began to chatter away, asking him a string of questions. He had to tell her how many goats he had, where he was taking them, and what he was going to do when he got there. Presently they reached the hut and came within Detie’s view. As soon as she spotted them she called out shrilly: ‘What on earth have you been doing, Heidi? What a sight you look! What have you done with your frocks? And the scarf? And those good new boots I bought you to come up here in, and the stockings I knitted for you? Wherever have you left them all?’ Heidi calmly pointed to the place where she had undressed.

translation: He dozed off on the bench, but his anxiety continued even in his sleep. Just before falling asleep, he remembered that Hippolytus would kill ten people, and he smiled at the absurdity of the assumption. Around him was a beautiful, clear silence, with only the rustling of leaves, from which it seemed that the silence became even quieter and more isolated. translation: Said the Monkey King attacked the door, but could not open it. He had to return to the Guanyin Temple. The monks in the temple had already buried the old monk, and were all attending Master Tang in the abbot's quarters. After finishing the morning repast, they laid out the noon repast. Just as they were about to add soup and change the water, the Monkey King descended from the void. The monks bowed down in reverence, ushered him into the abbot's quarters, and greeted Master Tang. Master Tang said, "The Monkey King has come. What about your robes?" The Monkey King said, "I've got a reason for it. This morning, I didn't wrong these monks after all. It was the black demon from Black Wind Mountain who stole them. Old Sun went quietly to search for him. He saw him and an elegant white-robed gentleman, as well as an old Taoist priest, sitting on a slope with grasses and flowers, discussing something. He was another one who wouldn't reveal himself. He suddenly said, 'Tomorrow is his mother's birthday, and he has invited all the demons to attend the celebration. Tonight he obtained a precious silk robe of the Buddha, which he wants to use for the occasion, to make a grand feast, which he calls the Celestial Tribute of the Buddha's Robe.' Old Sun seized the opportunity and struck him, causing the black demon to disperse into the wind. The Taoist priest disappeared as well, leaving only the white-robed gentleman, who was none other than a white snake with flowers transformed. I was in a hurry to follow him to his cave entrance and demand that he come out to fight with him. He admitted it, but said he took it back. We've been fighting for half a day, with neither side giving way. The demon retreated back into his cave and locked the stone door, not daring to come out. Old Sun returned to see his master, to report this news, and now the location of the robe is known. We're no longer afraid of him taking it." The monks heard the news, and all clasped their palms together and bowed their heads, murmuring "Amitabha Buddha! Today we've found the location, and we're finally safe!" The Monkey King said, "Don't be so elated, I still haven't got it in my hands yet, and Master hasn't left the temple yet. Let's just wait until I have the robe, and then I'll make sure Master leaves the temple safely and sound. Then and only then will you be truly safe. If there's the slightest risk, the Monkey King will not be trifled with! Has Master had a good meal and some good tea? Has Master's horse been fed some good grass?" The monks all eagerly agreed, saying, "Yes, yes, yes! We've never been remiss in serving the old master."
source_text: 却说行者攻门不开，也只得回观音院。那本寺僧人已葬埋了那老和尚，都在方丈里伏侍唐僧。早斋已毕，又摆上午斋，正那里添汤换水，只见行者从空降下，众僧礼拜，接入方丈，见了三藏。三藏道：“悟空你来了，袈裟如何？”行者道：“已有了根由。早是不曾冤了这些和尚，原来是那黑风山妖怪偷了。老孙去暗暗的寻他，只见他与一个白衣秀士，一个老道人，坐在那芳草坡前讲话。也是个不打自招的怪物，他忽然说出道：后日是他母难之日，邀请诸邪来做生日，夜来得了一件锦襕佛衣，要以此为寿，作一大宴，唤做庆赏佛衣会。是老孙抢到面前，打了一棍，那黑汉化风而走。道人也不见了，只把个白衣秀士打死，乃是一条白花蛇成精。我又急急赶到他洞口，叫他出来与他赌斗。他已承认了，是他拿回。战彀这半日，不分胜负。那怪回洞，却要吃饭，关了石门，惧战不出。老孙却来回看师父，先报此信，已是有了袈裟的下落，不怕他不还我。”众僧闻言，合掌的合掌，磕头的磕头，都念声“南无阿弥陀佛！今日寻着下落，我等方有了性命矣！”行者道：“你且休喜欢畅快，我还未曾到手，师父还未曾出门哩。只等有了袈裟，打发得我师父好好的出门，才是你们的安乐处；若稍有些须不虞，老孙可是好惹的主子！可曾有好茶饭与我师父吃？可曾有好草料喂马？”众僧俱满口答应道：“有！有！有！更不曾一毫有怠慢了老爷。”

translation:
"Master, here is the saddle and bridle," said Tripitaka after seeing them.  Tripitaka was overjoyed, received them, and handed them over to the pilgrim, who tried them on his back to see if they fitted. The pilgrim got off and took the things one by one to look at, and they were indeed some wonderful articles. To authenticate this, a poem was recited:

The saddle has intricate carvings flashing in the sun and shining with silver decorations, and the seat gleams with threads of gold. The cover has many layers of plush, folded in neat rows, and the reins are held by a cord of purple silk. The headstall has a leather cover with designs of flowers, while the fan has gold lines painting a beautiful animal. The bit is made of wrought iron, and the ends are reinforced with ends dipped in water, with a cord tied at the base. The pilgrim's heart was full of delight as he put the saddle and bridle on the horse, and it felt as if they had been made to order.

Tripitaka bowed to the old man, who hurried to help him up, saying, "No, no, it's nothing to thank for!" The old man did not wait for him to finish thanking, but invited him to mount. When the monk came out of the gate, he mounted his horse, and the pilgrim carried his luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a leather whip with a handle of fragrant creeper and a tip with tiger muscle silk, and offered it to him on the roadside, saying, "Holy monk, I've still got one whip left to present to you before you leave."

The monk on horseback took the whip and said, "Many thanks, many thanks!" Just as they were saying their goodbyes, the old man had disappeared from view, and when they looked back, they saw that the ground was empty. They heard a voice from the air saying, "Monk, don't be slow! I am the spirit of the mountain god of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to present the saddle and bridle to you two. You two should make good speed on your journey, but don't waste any time."

Tripitaka was so startled that he nearly fell off his horse. He dismounted, looked up in the air, and paid his respects, saying, "I, a disciple, am a mere mortal, do not recognize the holy spirit's face, and beg forgiveness for my offense. Please convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva for their kindness and blessings."

The monk kept bowing until he lost count, and at the roadside, the living Sun Wukong and the Monkey King were laughing and pleased, running up to grab Tripitaka's horse halter and say, "Master, get up! He's gone far away, you can't see or hear your prayers and prostrations. What's the point of bowing?"

In all, they number 35 works and 15,144 books, and are all sacred in that they show men how to be upright and good. All the knowledge of the four great continents, of the heavens, and the earth, of the races of men, of birds, and beasts, of flowers, of forestry and manufactures are complete in them. Since you have come a long distance, I must give you a complete set to carry back. But your people are ignorant and gross, calumniating the true scriptures and not understanding the deep meaning of our teachings. Call my two chief disciples, Ananda and Kasyapa. Let them lead these four travelers, first to the dining hall to dine, and then to the Library, and from each of the 35 works select a few to take back with them to circulate in the East.” Ananda and Kasyapa led them below, where they saw strange precious things in thousands. Gifts were provided for each of the pilgrims, and a vegetable banquet spread before them. All was of the very best, the choicest food, the most delicate tea, the finest fruit of all kinds, different from anything on earth among men. The Master and disciples raised the dishes to their heads in thanks for Buddha’s grace and then enjoyed them. Truly, their reigns golden light as bright as day, All kinds of nameless sweet incense, The eye meets a thousand trees in the beautiful palace, And the sweetest music charms the ear beyond all earthly strains, There the saints never grow old, Once partaking of celestial food, they live forever. All the sorrows of life are past, And now eternal glory and joy are attained. It was great bliss to Zhu Bajie and Sha the Monk to be at Buddha’s palace, and enjoy to their hearts’ content the banquet of immortals, who had cast off their mortal coils of bones and flesh and blood. Ananda and Kasyapa honored their guests with their presence. When their meal was over, the pilgrims were led to the Sacred Library, where books were stored in cupboards and boxes all with red labels of their names. After the four had seen the list of books, Ananda and Kasyapa said, if they were going to pay for the volumes, they would be given them at once. The Master replied that he had not been prepared to pay, as he understood the Scriptures were to be presented to them. The two smiled and said, “If we give away our Scriptures for nothing, we shall die of starvation.”

The master said, "The saddle and reins are presented." Three catties saw him, happy to receive them, and instructed Tripitaka to take them, to look at whether they fitted. Tripitaka walked forward, taking one thing after another to look at, and indeed they were some fine items. To prove it, it is said:

Carved saddle shines with rainbow lights, tassels of silver stars.
Treasure seat glitters with golden thread.
A layer of padding on the stool is filled with wool.
The ropes of three purple strings are tied.
The headstall is stitched with teaming flowers, a cloud fan painted with gold dancing beasts.
The rings are beaten from iron and polished to a shine, with two hangings drenched with water, and the hair-string decorations tied.
Tripitaka was secretly delighted, and placed the saddle and reins on the horse as if they had been made for him. 
Tripitaka bowed to thank the old man, the old man hurriedly helped him up, saying, "I was worried! I was worried! No need to trouble yourself to thank!"

The old man didn't stay to see Tripitaka get on the horse, and said to Tripitaka, "Come on!" 
The two old men came out of the door, mounted their horses, Tripitaka carried his luggage. The old man took out a whip from his sleeve, it was made of the bark of a fragrant vine, wrapped with tiger cord, and handed it over respectfully on the side of the road saying, "Holy monk, I have one more thing to give you, I'll give it to you on your way."

Tripitaka took the whip in his hand on the horse, saying, "Thank you for your generosity! Thank you for your generosity!"

Just as they were about to exchange greetings, the old man had already disappeared. When they looked back, the temple grounds were empty. Suddenly, they heard someone speaking from the air, saying, "Holy monk, don't hurry. I am the spirit of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and reins. You two can proceed with your journey, but don't be slow. "

The three of them were frightened and fell off the horse. They looked up and bowed, saying, "The disciple is but a human being with mortal flesh, and does not know the respect of the divine. I beg you to pardon me. Please convey this to the Bodhisattva, and bestow your blessings on me."

He just kept bowing, but didn't count the number of times. Just by their side, the Sun Wukong was laughing out loud, the Monkey King was delighted, and ran up to Tripitaka, grasping his robes, saying, "Teacher, get up, he's gone far away and can't hear you, he can't see you bowing. Just keep bowing like that."

Tripitaka said:

"Why are you laughing, my dear Sun Wukong? What are you laughing at? 

"Have you come to mock the laws of the monastery and to provoke the Bodhisattva? Then perhaps you won't get the monkey power after this journey. I'll be offended and won't save you.

"Your Reverence the Great Sage, let's get going, we have a long way to go.

"You know, when a mandarin duck flew to the skies, it's not just to soar, but also to sweep the waters below. If the fish and the birds see it, they'd know that the waters are sweet, so they'd come to live there. It's the same with you, Sun Wukong. You have the power of the Eight Lotus Flowers, why don't you just use it for your own benefits?

"As for me, I have promised the Bodhisattva to return to the capital, bring back the scriptures and spread the Buddhist teachings. My body is worn out, and I have a hundred thousand strands of silk that are far from rich.

"Please Sun Wukong, think about it with your great intelligence. When will we arrive in the Western Heavens? How will the world welcome the sacred scriptures? Don't forget the crowd of demon spirits and the various troubles on the road. Think with your wise head and decide on a plan. Why should we fly about without a thought?"

translation:
"Master, I present the saddle and bridle." The Three Caverns Master saw them and happily accepted them, teaching the Pilgrim to take them, and after mounting the horse, he looked and found them to be a suitable match. The Pilgrim walked up and one by one examined them, and indeed, they were fine things. There is a poem to attest to it, saying: 
The carved saddle gleams with vibrant colors, like stars in the silver moon.
The decorated stool radiates light, with golden threads shining bright.
A soft cloth draped on the tray, in several layers, tied with purple rope.
The rein head is made of a block of leather, with patterned flowers intricately crafted.
The cloud fan, with golden designs, depicts beasts dancing in the wind.
The metal ring clinks against the anvil, making the leather straps crisp.
The tips of the straps are dipped in water, with decorative hairs tied at the end.
The Pilgrim felt joy in his heart, and when he put the saddle and bridle on the horse, it looked as if they were made for him.

The Three Caverns Master bowed in gratitude, but the old man hurried to help him up and said, "Please, don't mention it! Please don't mention it!" The old man didn't invite him to stay, but instead bid the Three Caverns Master to mount his horse. The venerable monk left the gate, climbed onto his horse, and the Pilgrim carried the luggage. The old man took out a whip from his sleeve, a whip with a leather handle wrapped in scented cloth, with a piece of tiger sinew thread tied at the end, and offered it to the Three Caverns Master, saying, "Saintly monk, I still have one more gift for you, so please take it with you."

The Three Caverns Master was grateful and said, "Your benevolence is boundless! Your benevolence is boundless!" Just as he was about to ask for news, the old man had already disappeared, and when he looked back, the shrine was gone, and it was just a vast expanse of open land. Only then did he hear someone speaking from mid-air, saying, "Saintly monk, don't dawdle! I am the deity of the Mountain of Falling Flowers, sent by the Bodhisattva to present the saddle and bridle to you. You are to continue your journey to the West, but please don't delay."

The Three Caverns Master hastily got off his horse and bowed to the empty air, saying, "A disciple's ordinary mortal body cannot recognize the face of the noble deity, I beg your forgiveness. Please pass on my gratitude to the Bodhisattva, may they bestow their blessings upon me." He just kept bowing to the sky, without counting the number of bows, and on the side of the road, a living, laughing Sun Wukong and a delighted Monkey King appeared, and they came up to pull the Three Caverns Master up and said, "Master, get up! He's already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers and you can't see your bowing. Why keep bowing like that?"

source_text: “师父，鞍辔奉上。”三藏见了，欢喜领受，教行者拿了，背上马看，可相称否。行者走上前，一件件的取起看了，果然是些好物。有诗为证，诗曰：雕鞍彩晃柬银星，宝凳光飞金线明。衬屉几层绒苫迭，牵疆三股紫丝绳。辔头皮札团花粲，云扇描金舞兽形。环嚼叩成磨炼铁，两垂蘸水结毛缨。行者心中暗喜，将鞍辔背在马上，就似量着做的一般。三藏拜谢那老，那老慌忙搀起道：“惶恐！惶恐！何劳致谢？”那老者也不再留，请三藏上马。那长老出得门来，攀鞍上马，行者担着行李。那老儿复袖中取出一条鞭儿来，却是皮丁儿寸札的香藤柄子，虎筋丝穿结的梢儿，在路旁拱手奉上道：“圣僧，我还有一条挽手儿，一发送了你罢。”那三藏在马上接了道：“多承布施！多承布施！”正打问讯，却早不见了那老儿，及回看那里社祠，是一片光地。只听得半空中有人言语道：“圣僧，多简慢你。我是落伽山山神土地，蒙菩萨差送鞍辔与汝等的。汝等可努力西行，却莫一时怠慢。”慌得个三藏滚鞍下马，望空礼拜道：“弟子肉眼凡胎，不识尊神尊面，望乞恕罪。烦转达菩萨，深蒙恩佑。”你看他只管朝天磕头，也不计其数，路旁边活活的笑倒个孙大圣，孜孜的喜坏个美猴王，上前来扯住唐僧道：“师父，你起来罢，他已去得远了，听不见你祷祝，看不见你磕头。只管拜怎的？”长老道：

The Practitioner mounted his horse and looked at it to see if it was a good fit. The Practitioner walked forward and one by one, took up the pieces to look at them, and it indeed was some fine items. There was a poem as evidence, a poem that said:

The saddle carves, colors shining like stars, decorated with silver thread. 
The ornate bench shines, its gold lines radiant. 
A silken rug, layered like furs, folded and piled up. 
Three silk ropes, tightly tied with purple threads. 
The head of the bridle, a bundle of leather straps, adorned with colorful flowers. 
A fan, drawn in the image of cloud and beasts, is drawn with gold. 
The iron jawbiters, ground and polished, are suspended and hung with water-wet ends. 
The Practitioner's heart was secretly delighted, and he put the saddle and bridle on the horse as if they were custom-made. 

Three Cavern Saw Monks bowed to thank the old man, but the old man hastily helped him up and said, "Oh no, don't trouble yourself to thank me!" 
The old man didn't wait any longer, invited Three Cavern Saw Monks to mount his horse. Three Cavern Saw Monks came out of the door and mounted the horse, and the Practitioner carried his luggage. 
The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, a whip made from a piece of fragrant vine with a handle of leather strings and a tip of tiger's sinew, and handed it over to him, saying, "Saintly Monk, I have one more thing to give you, to send you off." 
Three Cavern Saw Monks in the horse replied, "I'm deeply grateful! I'm deeply grateful!" 

Just as he was about to ask a question, the old man had already disappeared. Upon looking back, the shrine was just a patch of empty land. 

Only to hear someone speaking from the air, "Saintly Monk, please don't be slow. I am the Land Deity of Luofa Mountain, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and bridle. You should hurry on your journey, but don't be too slow." 

The Practitioner was frightened and rolled down from the horse, looked up and kowtowed, saying, "Disciple, a mere mortal, didn't recognize the divine face, begging to be pardoned. Please ask the Bodhisattva to transmit my gratitude." 

He just kept banging his head against the ground, and did not count how many times. On the side of the road, the Monkey King and the Sun Wukong were alive, laughing and losing their joy, and came forward to grab hold of Three Cavern Saw Monks and said, "Father, get up, he's already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers or see you kowtowing. What are you still kowtowing for?"

The Practitioner said:

"What can be seen with the eyes can be reported with the mouth, if you speak of it it is like dust in the wind. 
If you only speak of it, it will be a false report, a mere story, and it cannot be related to the true state of things. 
If you say it, then it is like seeing smoke in the sky. 
If you don't say it, then it is like not seeing anything.

human_translations.translator_1: He set them down in the corridor, saying, “Master, I am presenting you with this harness.” When Tripitaka saw it, he accepted it with delight and asked Pilgrim to try the saddle on the horse. Going forward, Pilgrim took up the accoutrements and examined them piece by piece. They were indeed some magnificent articles, for which we have a testimonial poem. The poem says: The carved saddle shines with studs of silver stars. The precious seat glows with bright threads of gold. The pads are stacks of fine-spun woolen quilts. The reins are three bands of purple cords of silk. The bridle’s leather straps are shaped like flowers. The flaps have gold-etched forms of dancing beasts. The rings and bit are made of finest steel. Waterproof tassels dangle on both sides. Secretly pleased, Pilgrim put the saddle on the back of the horse, and it seemed to have been made to measure. Tripitaka bowed to thank the old man, who hastily raised him up, saying, “It’s nothing! What do you need to thank me for?” The old man did not ask them to stay any longer; instead, he urged Tripitaka to mount. The priest came out of the gate and climbed into the saddle, while Pilgrim followed, hauling the luggage. The old man then took a whip out from his sleeve, with a handle of rattan wrapped in strips of leather, and the strap knitted with cords made of tiger ligaments. He stood by the side of the road and presented it with hands uplifted, saying, “Holy Monk, I have a whip here that I may as well give you.” Tripitaka accepted it on his horse, saying, “Thanks for your donation! Thanks for your donation!” Even as he was saying this, the old man vanished. The priest turned around to look at the Lishe Shrine, but it had become just a piece of level ground. From the sky came a voice saying, “Holy Monk, I’m sorry not to have given you a better reception! I am the local spirit of Potalaka Mountain, who was sent by the Bodhisattva to present you with the harness. You two must journey to the West with all diligence. Do not be slothful in any moment.” Tripitaka was so startled that he fell off his horse and bowed toward the sky, saying, “Your disciple is of fleshly eyes and mortal stock, and he does not recognize the holy visage of the deity. Please forgive me. I beseech you to convey my gratitude to the Bodhisattva.” Look at him! All he could do was to kowtow toward the sky without bothering to count how many times! By the side of the road the Great Sage Sun reeled with laughter, the Handsome Monkey King broke up with hilarity. He came up and tugged at his master, saying, “Master, get up! He is long gone! He can’t hear you, nor can he see your kowtowing. Why keep up this adoration?”
human_translations.translator_2: Now I have three kinds of sacred books by which men can be delivered from their troubles and by which an end can be put to their sins. In all, they number 35 works and 15,144 books, and are all sacred in that they show men how to be upright and good. All the knowledge of the four great continents, of the heavens, and the earth, of the races of men, of birds, and beasts, of flowers, of forestry and manufactures are complete in them. Since you have come a long distance, I must give you a complete set to carry back. But your people are ignorant and gross, calumniating the true scriptures and not understanding the deep meaning of our teachings. Call my two chief disciples, Ananda and Kasyapa. Let them lead these four travelers, first to the dining hall to dine, and then to the Library, and from each of the 35 works select a few to take back with them to circulate in the East.” Ananda and Kasyapa led them below, where they saw strange precious things in thousands. Gifts were provided for each of the pilgrims, and a vegetable banquet spread before them. All was of the very best, the choicest food, the most delicate tea, the finest fruit of all kinds, different from anything on earth among men. The Master and disciples raised the dishes to their heads in thanks for Buddha’s grace and then enjoyed them. Truly, their reigns golden light as bright as day, All kinds of nameless sweet incense, The eye meets a thousand trees in the beautiful palace, And the sweetest music charms the ear beyond all earthly strains, There the saints never grow old, Once partaking of celestial food, they live forever. All the sorrows of life are past, And now eternal glory and joy are attained. It was great bliss to Zhu Bajie and Sha the Monk to be at Buddha’s palace, and enjoy to their hearts’ content the banquet of immortals, who had cast off their mortal coils of bones and flesh and blood. Ananda and Kasyapa honored their guests with their presence. When their meal was over, the pilgrims were led to the Sacred Library, where books were stored in cupboards and boxes all with red labels of their names. After the four had seen the list of books, Ananda and Kasyapa said, if they were going to pay for the volumes, they would be given them at once. The Master replied that he had not been prepared to pay, as he understood the Scriptures were to be presented to them. The two smiled and said, “If we give away our Scriptures for nothing, we shall die of starvation.”

translation:
The Master, I present the saddle and reins. Upon seeing him, the pilgrim expressed his joy and received them, then handed them over to the Traveller to carry. The Traveller looked at them on the horse and examined them one by one to see if they matched. The pilgrim walked up in front to inspect them, one by one, and, sure enough, they were some good things. There is a poem to attest to it, a poem that says:

The saddle shines with carved designs that sparkle like silver stars,
The upholstered cushions beam with light, with golden thread shining bright.
The covering has multiple layers of woolen cloth piled up, 
The three straps are made of purple silk threads.
The rein head is made of quilted leather with flowers embroidered on it,
The cloud fan has golden decorations depicting beasts in motion.
The iron jawbone is hammered into shape, the two tassels are dipped in water, tied with horsehair.
The pilgrim was secretly delighted, and as he put the saddle and reins on the horse, it was just like they were made to fit.

The pilgrim bowed to thank the old man, but the old man hastily helped him up and said, "No need to thank me, no need to thank me, it's no trouble at all!" The old man no longer lingered, and invited the pilgrim to mount his horse. The venerable monk then left the gate, mounted his horse, and the Traveller carried his luggage. The old man then took out a whip from his sleeve, it was made of a strip of aromatic cinnamon bark about an inch thick, with tiger tendon strings tied at the end, and handed it to him with a bow, saying, "Holy monk, I still have a gift for you, please accept it as a parting gift."

The pilgrim on horseback accepted it and said, "I am grateful, I am grateful!" Just as they were about to bid farewell, the old man was gone, and when they looked back, the temple was empty. They could hear someone speaking in mid-air saying, "Holy monk, please hurry along, do not tarry! I am the land god of Mount Luofu, sent by the Bodhisattva to give you the saddle and reins. Please hurry along on your journey, do not tarry."

The pilgrim rolled off his horse in a hurry, gazing upwards to pay his respects and saying, "I, a humble disciple, am blind to the majesty of the gods and do not recognize your divine visage, I beg for your pardon. Please pass on my thanks to the Bodhisattva and bestow your benevolence upon me." The pilgrim went on, not counting how many times he bowed, and, to the side, a living figure of the Monkey King was laughing out loud and a smiling Sun Wukong was grinning, they both came up and pulled at the pilgrim's sleeves saying, "Father, please get up, he has already gone far away, you can't hear your prayers and can't see your bows, just stop bowing like this!"

The pilgrim said, "Old Master, why did the land god of Mount Luofu come to bless us and give us the saddle and reins?"
